policies.purpose: To protect the privacy of residents and the confidentiality of their health and personal information, while keeping records at the facility and readily available to AHCA as required.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] keeps resident records at the licensee's physical address, ready for AHCA inspection, as required by Rule 59A-36.015, F.A.C. Resident information is confidential. The facility releases information only with the resident's (or legal representative's) written authorization, or when the law requires or permits it, such as to AHCA surveyors, the Ombudsman, protective services investigators, law enforcement acting under legal authority, or emergency medical providers. If the facility is a HIPAA covered entity, it follows 45 CFR 164.530 (administrative requirements, including a privacy official, training, safeguards, and complaint process) and 45 CFR 164.524 (resident right of access to records). If the facility is not a covered entity, it applies the same standards as its confidentiality policy. Residents have privacy during personal care, in their mail and telephone use, and in visits with others.

definitions.definition: Individually identifiable information about a resident's health, care, or payment, in any form.
A health care provider, plan, or clearinghouse that is subject to HIPAA.
A signed, dated written permission from the resident or legal representative to release specific information to a specific person.
The staff member designated to oversee privacy compliance: [PRIVACY OFFICER NAME].

procedures: The Administrator designates a Privacy Officer ([PRIVACY OFFICER NAME]) and records the designation in writing.

The Administrator determines whether the facility is a HIPAA covered entity (for example, by billing health plans electronically) and records the determination. If it is not, the facility follows this policy as its confidentiality standard.
All staff, volunteers, and contractors sign a confidentiality agreement at hire and receive privacy training at orientation and annually (STF-03). Training is documented.

Resident records are kept at the facility's physical address [ADDRESS], in locked cabinets or in a password-protected electronic system. Access is limited to staff who need the information to do their job.
Staff do not leave records, medication administration records, or screens open or unattended where visitors or other residents can see them.
Staff discuss resident information only where others cannot overhear, and never on social media or in public.

Staff release information only with a signed authorization from the resident or legal representative, or as required or permitted by law. Staff check the identity of the requester and refer unclear requests to the Administrator or Privacy Officer.

Staff ask for proof of the authority of any representative, such as a health care surrogate, guardian, or power of attorney, before sharing information with that person, and file the proof in the record.

When AHCA surveyors, the Ombudsman, or other authorized agency representatives ask to see records, staff notify the Administrator or person in charge, who provides access promptly. The release is logged.
The facility gives each resident a notice of privacy practices if it is a covered entity, and explains in plain language how information is used and shared.

A resident or representative may ask to see or get a copy of the record. The Administrator or Privacy Officer responds in writing within 30 days (or any shorter period required by law) and records the request and the response. Reasonable cost-based fees are told in advance.
Staff protect residents' privacy during bathing, dressing, toileting, and treatment: knock, close doors and curtains, and expose only what is necessary.
Residents' mail is delivered unopened. Residents may use a telephone privately and receive visitors privately, within house rules that do not limit residents' rights (RR-01, SAF-14).

Staff keep photographs, video, or recordings of residents only with the resident's written consent, except for security cameras in common areas as disclosed in the admission package (cameras are not placed in bedrooms or bathrooms).

Staff report any suspected breach (lost record, wrong recipient, unauthorized access) to the Privacy Officer immediately. The Privacy Officer investigates, notifies the resident, and takes corrective action. For a covered entity, the Privacy Officer also decides if notification is required by law. The event is documented.
The facility follows the retention and disposal requirements of REC-01 and destroys records securely (shredding or secure electronic deletion) only when retention periods have passed.
Staff who violate this policy are subject to discipline, up to termination (STF-06).

responsibilities.duty: Designates the Privacy Officer, ensures safeguards, and makes records available to AHCA at the physical address.
Handles access requests, authorizations, breach reviews, and training content.
Keep resident information confidential, share only as allowed, and report breaches.

documentation: Privacy Officer designation and covered-entity determination
Signed confidentiality agreements and training records
Signed authorizations for release
Access request log and responses
Breach and incident reports
Record disposal log

policies.title: Nondiscrimination and Language Access
policies.applies_to: All staff, volunteers, and contractors; applicants, residents, and representatives
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] admits, serves, and retains residents on the basis of the criteria in the state rules and the facility's ability to meet their needs, and not on the basis of any protected characteristic. To make sure residents who have limited English or a disability can understand and use the facility's services and information.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] does not discriminate on the basis of race, color, national origin, religion, sex, age, disability, source of payment, or any other characteristic protected by law, in admission, services, room assignment, discharge, or any other aspect of residency. This is consistent with Title VI of the Civil Rights Act (42 USC 2000d), the Americans with Disabilities Act (42 USC 12101 et seq.), and the Resident Bill of Rights in s. 429.28, F.S., which protects residents' right to live free of discrimination and with dignity. Admission and retention decisions are made only under the criteria in Rule 59A-36.006, F.A.C. (see ADM-01, ADM-05). The facility provides interpreter services or translated materials on request, at no charge to the resident, and makes reasonable accommodations for residents with disabilities.

definitions.definition: A limited ability to read, speak, write, or understand English well enough to take part in services.

A change in rules, policies, practices, or services, or a modification to the physical setting, that gives a person with a disability an equal chance to use and enjoy the facility, unless it would be an undue burden or fundamental alteration.
A trait for which the law prohibits discrimination, as listed in this policy.

procedures: The Administrator posts a nondiscrimination statement in the common area and includes it in the admission package (ADM-02). The statement tells residents how to file a discrimination complaint with the facility (RR-02) and with outside agencies.

Admissions staff evaluate every applicant using the same written criteria in ADM-01 and Rule 59A-36.006, F.A.C. They do not turn away or delay an applicant because of a protected characteristic or source of payment.

If an applicant is declined, the Administrator documents the specific admission criterion that is not met or the specific service the facility cannot provide, and tells the applicant or representative the reason in writing.
Staff use the same criteria in retention and discharge decisions (ADM-05, ADM-06). A discharge for reasons other than the criteria in the rule is not permitted.
At first contact, staff ask each applicant and resident what language he or she prefers for spoken and written information and record the answer in the record.

When a resident or representative asks for, or appears to need, language help, staff arrange an interpreter (a qualified bilingual staff member, a telephone or video interpreter service, or a community interpreter) at no charge. Staff do not ask or expect family members or other residents to interpret, except if the resident requests it and the reliability of the family member is confirmed, or in an emergency until a qualified interpreter is available.

The Administrator keeps key documents, including the contract, grievance procedure, Bill of Rights, house rules, and complaint notices, available in the primary languages of the people the facility serves, and arranges a translation or sight-translation when a resident needs another language.

For a resident with a hearing, vision, speech, cognitive, or mobility disability, staff ask what help the resident needs and provide it as a reasonable accommodation: for example, large-print or read-aloud materials, written communication, hearing devices, accessible rooms, or modifications of a rule.
The Administrator decides requests for accommodation promptly, documents the request and decision, and explains any denial in writing, along with the alternatives offered.
Service animals are allowed as the law requires for people with disabilities (see SAF-14 for pets).
Staff respect residents' cultural, religious, and dietary practices in care, meals (DL-01), and activities (DL-02) to the extent possible and record preferences in the service plan (ADM-04).
Staff must not use slurs, harassment, or demeaning treatment on any basis. Reports are made to the Administrator, who investigates under RR-02 and takes corrective action, up to termination (STF-06).
Residents who believe they have been discriminated against may complain to the facility, to the Ombudsman, to AHCA, or to other civil rights agencies. Retaliation is prohibited.
The Administrator trains all staff on this policy at orientation and annually (STF-03), and reviews language and accommodation requests quarterly as part of quality assurance (GOV-03).

responsibilities.duty: Ensures nondiscriminatory admission and retention decisions, arranges language services and accommodations, and investigates complaints.
Apply written criteria consistently, document the reasons for any decline, and record language preference.
Treat all residents with respect, use qualified interpreters, and report discrimination.

documentation: Posted nondiscrimination statement and admission package copy
Admission screening decisions and written reasons for any decline
Language preference record and interpreter use log
Translated materials on file
Accommodation requests, decisions, and denials
Grievance records on discrimination complaints
Training records

policies.title: Pre-Admission Screening and Admission Criteria
policies.applies_to: All [AGENCY NAME] licensure types: standard ALF, and Extended Congregate Care (ECC), Limited Nursing Services (LNS) and Limited Mental Health (LMH) specialty licenses, to the extent held
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] admits only applicants whose needs it can safely meet with the services it provides or arranges, and that the administrator's admission decision rests on written criteria and a documented screening.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] admits a person only after a documented pre-admission screening and a written appropriateness determination by the Administrator. This policy meets Rule 59A-36.006(1)(a)15.c., F.A.C. (the facility's admission policy and the services the facility is prepared to provide or arrange, which is the basis for the Administrator's appropriateness determination). It also meets Rule 59A-36.006(3)(a)1., F.A.C. (the facility's admission and continued residency criteria, given to every resident in the admission package). Admission criteria: (a) the applicant is 18 years of age or older; (b) the applicant can perform activities of daily living with assistance, whether from facility staff or arranged providers, and can transfer with help; (c) the applicant is not bedridden, except under the hospice provision of Rule 59A-36.006 and s. 429.26, F.S.; (d) the applicant has no stage 3 or stage 4 pressure sores; (e) the applicant does not require any of the nursing services or conditions listed in Rule 59A-36.006(1) as excluding admission, unless the facility holds the license (ECC or LNS) that permits the service and has the staff to provide it; (f) the applicant does not require 24-hour licensed mental health treatment; and (g) the Administrator finds that the applicant's needs are within the services [AGENCY NAME] provides or arranges and within its license. Continued residency criteria are in ADM-05. The admission policy and continued residency criteria are given to each applicant at or before admission under ADM-02. [AGENCY NAME] does not discriminate in admission (RR-07).

definitions.definition: The Administrator's written finding, made from the screening and the medical examination information, that the applicant meets the admission criteria and that the facility can meet the applicant's needs.
The documented review of an applicant's health, functional, behavioral and social needs before an admission decision.

definitions.term: Services the facility is prepared to provide or arrange
definitions.definition: The written list of personal care, nursing (if licensed), dietary, transportation and other services stated in the admission package and contract.
The person legally authorized to act for the resident, such as a health care surrogate, agent under a power of attorney, or guardian.

procedures: The Administrator or designee takes each inquiry and gives the applicant and family the current admission package (ADM-02) or tells them where to get it.

Before admission, the Administrator or designee completes the Pre-Admission Screening form [FORM NAME]. It is based on an interview with the applicant and representative and a review of records from the referring hospital, physician or agency.

The screening records age, diagnoses, medications, ability to perform ADLs, transfer ability, mobility and fall history, continence, skin condition (including any pressure sores and their stage), cognition and wandering or elopement risk, behaviors, mental health history, nutrition and diet orders, and any current nursing or treatment needs.
The screener checks each admission criterion in the Policy section on the Admission Criteria Checklist and marks it met or not met.

If the applicant has a stage 3 or 4 pressure sore, is bedridden (other than under hospice), or needs a service listed in Rule 59A-36.006(1) that the facility's license does not allow, the Administrator declines admission and records the reason.

If the applicant appears to need 24-hour licensed mental health treatment, the Administrator declines admission and refers the applicant or representative to appropriate community mental health resources.

If the applicant needs a service that [AGENCY NAME] does not provide but could arrange (for example home health, hospice or therapy), the Administrator confirms before admission that a licensed third-party provider is available and that the resident or representative agrees to the arrangement and its cost.
For applicants with ECC, LNS or LMH needs, the Administrator confirms that the facility holds that license, has the required staff or contracted nurse, and can meet the needs (HS-09, HS-03, HS-11).
The Administrator makes and signs the written appropriateness determination, with the date and the reasons, and files it with the screening before the admission date.

The Administrator confirms that the face-to-face medical examination is scheduled or complete within the time allowed (ADM-03). A resident whose exam findings show they do not meet the criteria is not admitted, or is assessed under ADM-05 if already in residence.

The Administrator tells the applicant and representative of the decision. If admission is declined, this is done the same business day when possible, with the reason and, where appropriate, referral information. A written notice is kept.
If admission is approved, the Administrator offers the admission package and contract (ADM-02, RR-03) at or before admission and records the signed receipt.
The Administrator reviews screening decisions quarterly as part of quality assurance (GOV-03) to confirm criteria were applied consistently, and updates this policy when rules change (GOV-02).
Screening records are kept in the resident's record for admitted residents, and in an inquiry/declined-admission file for [RETENTION PERIOD] for applicants who are not admitted.

responsibilities.duty: Makes and signs each appropriateness determination, declines applicants who do not meet criteria, and ensures this policy is applied consistently.
Completes the screening and checklist, gathers records, and gives the admission package.
Reviews the screening for nursing needs and advises the Administrator whether those needs fall within the license.
Provides accurate health and functional information and records.

documentation: Pre-Admission Screening form
Admission Criteria Checklist
Administrator's signed appropriateness determination
Declined-admission notices and referral notes
Records received from referring providers

policies.title: Admission Package and Required Disclosures
policies.applies_to: All [AGENCY NAME] licensure types (standard, ECC, LNS, LMH), with additional disclosures where the facility holds an ECC license or serves residents with Alzheimer's disease or related disorders
policies.purpose: To make sure every applicant and representative receives, at or before admission, the written information they need to decide about residency, and that [AGENCY NAME] can show receipt.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] gives every applicant or representative a written admission package at or before admission and obtains a signed, dated receipt. The package is kept current and meets Rule 59A-36.006(3)(a), F.A.C., as follows. Item 59A-36.006(3)(a)1.: the facility's admission and continued residency criteria (ADM-01, ADM-05). Item (3)(a)2.: the daily, weekly or monthly charge and the services, supplies and accommodations included in that rate. Item (3)(a)3.: personal care services the facility is prepared to provide and any additional cost. Item (3)(a)4.: nursing services the facility is prepared to provide and any additional cost, with a statement of the facility's LNS and/or ECC license status. Item (3)(a)5.: food service and the facility's ability to accommodate special diets. Item (3)(a)6.: availability of transportation and any additional cost. Item (3)(a)7.: any other special services and their cost. Item (3)(a)8.: the social and leisure activities generally offered. Item (3)(a)9.: services the facility does not provide but will arrange, with any additional cost. Item (3)(a)10.: the facility rules and regulations residents must follow, as described in Rule 59A-36.007, F.A.C. (house rules, RR-01). Item (3)(a)11.: the facility's policy on Do Not Resuscitate Orders under s. 429.255, F.S. and Rule 59A-36.009, F.A.C., and on advance directives under Chapter 765, F.S. (RR-05). The Resident Contract under Rule 59A-36.018 and s. 429.24, F.S. is offered before or at admission (RR-03). Additional disclosures: if the facility holds an ECC license, a description of ECC services and the criteria under which they are provided; if the facility serves residents with Alzheimer's disease or related disorders, a description of the special services and the elopement policy; and any rule requiring central storage of resident medications, as permitted by Rule 59A-36.008(6)(b)6., F.A.C.

definitions.definition: The written materials described in this policy, given to the applicant or representative at or before admission.
Any charge not included in the base rate. Additional charges require an itemized statement and a signed, dated contract addendum (RR-03).
A facility practice of keeping residents' medications in a locked area controlled by staff, as allowed by Rule 59A-36.008(6)(b)6. and HS-01.
Services delivered by a third party (for example home health, hospice, therapy or a pharmacy) that the facility helps the resident obtain.

procedures: The Administrator maintains one current Admission Package containing all items in the Policy section, with a table of contents that cross-references each item to Rule 59A-36.006(3)(a)1. through 11.
The Administrator reviews the package at least annually, and whenever rates, services, house rules, licenses or applicable rules change, and records the date and reviewer on the revision page.

The package states the base rate and what it includes, and lists each personal care service, nursing service (if any), special diet, transportation option, activity and other service. Each is labelled 'included' or shown with a price.
The package lists services the facility does not provide but will arrange, with who provides them and the cost to the resident, and says that arranging does not make [AGENCY NAME] the provider.
The package includes the current house rules (RR-01), the DNRO and advance directive policy (RR-05), and the Resident Bill of Rights and grievance information (RR-01, RR-02).

If the facility holds an ECC license, the Administrator adds the ECC description and criteria (HS-09, HS-10). If the facility serves residents with Alzheimer's disease or related disorders, the Administrator adds the description of special services and the elopement policy (HS-05, SAF-03).
If the facility keeps resident medications in central storage, the package states this rule and explains how residents who self-administer can access their medications (HS-01).

The Admissions Coordinator gives the full package, plus the Resident Contract, to the applicant or representative at or before admission. The Admissions Coordinator explains each section in plain language and, where needed, with an interpreter or translated materials (RR-07).
The Admissions Coordinator gives the applicant time to read the package and ask questions, and answers questions or refers them to the Administrator.
The applicant or representative signs and dates the Admission Package Receipt, which lists every item in the package. The Admissions Coordinator signs as witness.
The resident or representative receives a copy of the signed contract and any signed addendum. The Administrator ensures that a copy is in the resident record.
If the applicant or representative will not sign the receipt, the Admissions Coordinator records the refusal and the date and time the package was given, and tells the Administrator.

When any item in the package changes for an existing resident, the Administrator gives the written change to the resident or representative, with the notice required in the contract (30 days for rate increases), and documents it. Additional charges are added only by itemized statement and signed, dated addendum.
The Administrator audits the files of all new admissions each month for a completed receipt and contract, and reports findings to the quality assurance committee (GOV-03).

responsibilities.duty: Keeps the package current and complete, approves changes, and audits new admission files.
Delivers and explains the package, obtains the signed receipt, and files it.
Helps the Administrator describe nursing services, their cost and their limits accurately.
Reviews the package and signs the receipt.

documentation: Current Admission Package with revision log
Signed and dated Admission Package Receipt
Signed Resident Contract and addenda
Itemized statements for additional charges
Refusal-to-sign notes, if any
Monthly admission file audit

policies.title: Resident Assessment, Medical Examination and Reassessment
policies.applies_to: All [AGENCY NAME] residents and licensure types (standard, ECC, LNS, LMH)
policies.purpose: To make sure each resident has a timely face-to-face medical examination and a documented assessment on admission, at required intervals, and after a significant change, so that care and continued residency decisions are based on current information.
policies.policy: Each resident must have a face-to-face medical examination by a licensed practitioner within 60 days before admission or within 30 days after admission, as required by Rule 59A-36.006 and s. 429.26(5), F.S. The examination is recorded on AHCA Form 1823 or on the practitioner's own form that contains the required information. The resident is re-examined at least every 3 years and after any significant change in condition. The practitioner's findings on the resident's ability to self-administer medication are recorded in the resident record. Staff document each significant change in condition in the record (Rule 59A-36.007(1)). The Administrator reviews the exam findings against the continued residency criteria (ADM-05) and reassesses the resident after hospitalization or a significant change. Staff who perform observations and assessments are trained under Rule 59A-36.011 (STF-03).

definitions.definition: The Resident Health Assessment for Assisted Living Facilities, the state form on which a practitioner records the medical examination.
A person licensed in Florida to perform the examination, such as a physician, physician assistant or advanced practice registered nurse, acting within their scope.

A change in the resident's physical, mental or functional condition that is likely to affect the services needed or the resident's ability to continue to reside in the facility, such as new or worsening ADL dependence, a new diagnosis, a new pressure sore, unexplained weight loss, a fall with injury, a new behavior, or a hospitalization.
The resident's ability to take their own medication without staff administering it, as found by the practitioner (HS-02).

procedures: At the pre-admission screening (ADM-01), the Admissions Coordinator asks the applicant or representative whether a medical examination has been done in the last 60 days. If not, they give them Form 1823 for the practitioner to complete.
The Administrator records the exam due date on the Admission Tracking Sheet: no earlier than 60 days before and no later than 30 days after the admission date.

On receipt, the Administrator or designee checks Form 1823 (or the practitioner's form) for the exam date, the practitioner's signature and license information, diagnoses, current medications, diet, ability to perform ADLs, any bedridden status or pressure sores, and whether the resident needs nursing services.

The Administrator or designee checks that the practitioner has recorded whether the resident can self-administer medication, and files that finding in the record. If it is blank, they contact the practitioner for completion before the resident self-administers or staff assist (HS-02).

If the exam is not completed within 30 days after admission, the Administrator contacts the practitioner and the representative the day the deadline passes, documents the follow-up, and arranges for an exam as soon as possible. The Administrator then reviews whether continued residency is appropriate.

Within 7 days of admission, a trained staff member completes the facility's admission assessment [FORM NAME] covering functional ability, personal preferences, fall risk, skin condition, nutrition and behaviors. The Administrator signs it.

The Administrator reviews the exam and assessment together against the continued residency criteria (ADM-05) and documents whether the resident remains appropriate. If not, the Administrator follows ADM-05 and ADM-06.

Staff record any significant change in a resident's condition in the resident record on the day it is observed, and tell the Administrator or nurse the same shift (HS-04). The Administrator documents the review and action taken.

After a hospital stay, emergency visit or any significant change, the Administrator or licensed nurse reassesses the resident within [TIMEFRAME, no later than 3 business days] after the change or return, reviews discharge orders and medication changes, and updates the service plan (ADM-04).

The Administrator arranges for a new face-to-face medical examination at least every 3 years, and after any significant change when the practitioner needs to confirm the resident's condition. The Administrator tracks due dates on the Reassessment Calendar and starts the request 60 days before each due date.

If the resident has a significant change that suggests a need for services beyond the facility's license, the Administrator consults the resident's practitioner, the resident and the representative, and applies ADM-05.
The Administrator reports reassessment completion rates, and any late examinations, to the quality assurance committee quarterly (GOV-03).

responsibilities.duty: Tracks exam deadlines, reviews findings against continued residency criteria, and decides on action after significant change.

responsibilities.role: Licensed Nurse (ECC/LNS) or designated trained staff
responsibilities.duty: Perform assessments and reassessments, document changes, and notify the practitioner as needed.
Observe and report changes in condition on the same shift.
Arrange the medical examination and provide complete information.

documentation: AHCA Form 1823 or practitioner's form
Admission Tracking Sheet and Reassessment Calendar
Admission assessment and reassessments
Records of significant changes and follow-up
Practitioner findings on self-administration of medication
Follow-up notes for late examinations

policies.title: Service Plan / Care Plan
policies.applies_to: All [AGENCY NAME] residents; additional requirements for residents under ECC, LNS and LMH licenses
policies.purpose: To make sure each resident has an individualized written plan, developed with the resident and representative, that states the services provided and arranged, and that the plan is reviewed and updated as the licensed specialty services require.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] develops a written service/care plan for every resident from the admission assessment and medical examination, with the resident and representative taking part. The plan states the resident's needs, preferences, and the services staff or third parties will provide, and who is responsible. Supervision, and a written record of significant changes, follow Rule 59A-36.007(1). ECC: for residents receiving ECC services, the plan is reviewed quarterly and a licensed nurse completes monthly nursing assessments (Rule 59A-36.021). LNS: nursing services are provided only on a practitioner's order, and a licensed nurse completes monthly nursing assessments and nursing progress notes (Rule 59A-36.022). LMH: for each resident with a mental health diagnosis, the facility keeps a community living support plan and a cooperative agreement with the resident's mental health provider (Rule 59A-36.020). Restraints: no physical restraint is used without a care plan that meets Rule 59A-36.007(8) (SAF-04). Third-party services (home health, hospice, therapy) are coordinated and communicated under Rule 59A-36.007(6). Assistive devices are addressed in the plan under Rule 59A-36.007(9).

definitions.definition: The written, individualized plan of the resident's services, supports, supervision level and goals.
A licensed nurse's documented review of the resident's health and the services under ECC or LNS, completed every month.
The plan for an LMH resident describing the supports needed for living in the community, developed with the mental health provider.
The written agreement between the facility and the resident's mental health case manager or provider on coordination of care.

procedures: Within [TIMEFRAME, no later than 7 days] of admission, the Administrator or nurse meets with the resident and representative to draft the service/care plan from the screening, exam and assessment (ADM-01, ADM-03).

The plan lists the resident's ADL assistance needs, supervision level, medication assistance or self-administration status, diet, mobility and assistive devices, fall and skin risks, behaviors, activity preferences, and communication needs.
The plan names each service, who provides it (facility staff or third party), how often, and any additional cost, consistent with the Resident Contract (RR-03).
The resident, representative and Administrator sign the plan, or the record states why a signature was not obtained. The resident gets a copy.
Direct care staff are told of the plan and have access to the current version, with instructions that are specific to the resident.

ECC residents: a licensed nurse completes a nursing assessment every month and documents it. The Administrator, nurse, resident and representative review the service plan every quarter and whenever needs change, and the updated plan is signed (HS-09, HS-10).
LNS residents: the nurse provides only nursing services ordered by a practitioner, files the order in the record, completes a monthly nursing assessment and writes nursing progress notes (HS-03).

LMH residents: before admission and at least [FREQUENCY] thereafter, the Administrator confirms that the resident has a community living support plan and a cooperative agreement with the mental health provider, files both, and updates the service plan to match (HS-11).
Staff record significant changes in condition and notify the Administrator or nurse the same shift, and the plan is updated within [TIMEFRAME, no later than 3 business days] (ADM-03, HS-04).

When a third-party provider such as home health or hospice serves a resident, the Administrator obtains the provider's plan of care, coordinates it with the service plan, and communicates changes to the provider in writing (HS-07).
If a physical restraint is ordered, the Administrator confirms that the resident's care plan meets Rule 59A-36.007(8) and follows SAF-04 before any use.
The Administrator reviews a sample of plans each quarter for completeness and timeliness, and reports results to the quality assurance committee (GOV-03).

responsibilities.duty: Ensures each plan is developed, signed, reviewed and implemented, and that specialty-license requirements are met.
Completes monthly nursing assessments and progress notes, and participates in quarterly ECC reviews.
Follow the plan and report changes or refusals of care.
Take part in the plan and review it.
Provides and updates the community living support plan and cooperates under the agreement.

documentation: Signed service/care plan and revisions
Monthly nursing assessments and progress notes (ECC/LNS)
Quarterly ECC plan review record
Practitioner orders for nursing services
Community living support plan and cooperative agreement (LMH)
Restraint care plan, if any
Third-party provider plans and communications

policies.title: Retention Limits and Conditions the Facility Cannot Serve
policies.applies_to: All [AGENCY NAME] residents; exceptions apply only within the ECC and LNS licensed scope
policies.purpose: To state the conditions under which a resident can continue to live at [AGENCY NAME], the conditions that require a different level of care, and the steps the Administrator takes when a resident's needs change.
policies.policy: A resident may remain at [AGENCY NAME] only while the resident continues to meet the continued residency criteria in Rule 59A-36.006, F.A.C., and the facility can meet the resident's needs. A resident who is bedridden for more than 7 consecutive days, who develops a stage 3 or 4 pressure sore, or who needs a nursing service listed in Rule 59A-36.006(1) as excluding residency, may not remain unless an exception below applies. Exceptions: (a) a resident who is receiving hospice services may be bedridden and may be retained under the hospice provisions of Rule 59A-36.006 and s. 429.26(1), F.S., provided the facility and hospice agree to a plan of care and the facility can meet the resident's needs (HS-07); (b) a terminally ill resident may be retained under the conditions of Rule 59A-36.006(4), including that hospice or other required services are in place; (c) a resident with a stage 2 pressure sore may remain only where the conditions of Rule 59A-36.006(4) are met and care is given within the facility's licensed scope or by a licensed third-party provider; and (d) nursing services that would otherwise exclude a resident may be provided only if the facility holds the ECC or LNS license that allows them, has the nurse and staffing required by Rule 59A-36.021 or 59A-36.022, and the resident's needs are within that license. [AGENCY NAME] does not retain a resident whose needs it cannot safely meet because of staffing, license scope or physical plant. When a resident no longer meets criteria, the Administrator acts under ADM-06.

definitions.definition: Unable to get out of bed without the assistance of more than one person or confined to bed due to a medical condition, for the purposes of this policy as defined in the rule. A resident who is bedridden for more than 7 consecutive days no longer meets continued residency criteria, except under hospice.
The staging used in the practitioner's or nurse's assessment. Stage 3 and 4 sores exclude residency. Stage 2 sores may be retained only on rule conditions.
A resident with a life expectancy of less than 1 year who, if retained, receives care under the rule conditions, including hospice.
The services [AGENCY NAME] may lawfully provide under its standard, ECC, LNS or LMH license.

procedures: Staff report to the Administrator or nurse, the same shift, any resident who is confined to bed, has a skin breakdown, or shows a new need for nursing care (ADM-03, HS-04, HS-06).
The Administrator or nurse records the date the resident became bedridden, and a running count of consecutive days, on the Retention Watch log.
On the day a resident is first confined to bed, the Administrator tells the resident's practitioner and the representative, and asks for a medical evaluation and a plan of care.

If the resident is still bedridden at day 5, the Administrator reviews with the practitioner and representative whether recovery is expected before day 7, and begins planning for transfer or hospice referral.
If a resident remains bedridden after 7 consecutive days and is not receiving hospice, the Administrator starts the discharge or transfer process under ADM-06 and records the reason.
If a pressure sore is found, the nurse or designee records its stage and location, notifies the practitioner the same day, and begins the care plan changes (HS-06).
If a sore is stage 3 or 4, the Administrator starts the discharge or transfer process under ADM-06 and arranges immediate medical care.

If a sore is stage 2, the Administrator confirms that the Rule 59A-36.006(4) conditions are met, that a practitioner order and treatment plan exist, and that a licensed nurse or licensed third-party provider provides the care. If they cannot be met, the Administrator starts ADM-06.

When a resident is terminally ill, the Administrator, the resident or representative and the practitioner decide whether to retain the resident with hospice. They sign a written plan with the hospice agency (HS-07), and the Administrator confirms the conditions in Rule 59A-36.006(4) are met before continued stay.

When a resident needs a nursing service that excludes residency, the Administrator first checks whether the facility holds ECC or LNS licensure that permits it, whether the nurse and staffing are in place, and whether the service is ordered by a practitioner (HS-03, HS-09). If the facility cannot meet these requirements, ADM-06 applies.
The Administrator documents each retention decision, the facts and the rule basis, in the resident record, and tells the resident and representative in writing.
If the resident or representative disagrees with the Administrator's determination, the Administrator follows s. 429.26(8), F.S., as set out in ADM-06.
The Administrator reviews the Retention Watch log each month, and reports retention decisions and discharges for care-need reasons to the quality assurance committee (GOV-03).

responsibilities.duty: Makes retention decisions, tracks bedridden days and conditions, and starts discharge or transfer when criteria are not met.
Assesses skin and nursing needs, confirms orders and licensed scope, and advises the Administrator.
Report bedridden status, skin changes and new care needs the same shift.
Evaluates the resident, writes orders and advises on appropriateness.
Provides hospice services and shares the plan of care with the facility.

documentation: Retention Watch log
Skin assessments and practitioner orders
Hospice agreement and plan of care
Administrator's written retention decision
Notices to the resident and representative
ECC/LNS orders, nursing assessments

policies.title: Discharge, Transfer and Relocation Notice
policies.applies_to: All [AGENCY NAME] residents and licensure types
policies.purpose: To make sure any discharge, transfer or relocation is based on a documented reason, follows the notice terms in the Resident Contract, protects the resident's safety and rights, and results in proper refunds and records.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] discharges or transfers a resident only for a reason stated in the Resident Contract and permitted by Rule 59A-36.006(5), F.A.C., and Chapter 429, F.S.: for example, when the resident no longer meets continued residency criteria (ADM-05), when the facility cannot meet the resident's needs, for nonpayment, or when the resident chooses to leave. The transfer notice terms appear in the Resident Contract as required by Rule 59A-36.018 and s. 429.24, F.S. The written notice period is the one stated in the contract, and [AGENCY NAME] will not set it shorter than the period required by Rule 59A-36.006(5) and Rule 59A-36.018. Disagreements about the appropriateness of placement are handled under s. 429.26(8), F.S. Refunds of deposits and prepaid amounts follow the contract and s. 429.24, F.S. Every admission and discharge is entered in the admission/discharge log required by Rule 59A-36.015, F.A.C. The facility will not discharge a resident in retaliation for exercising resident rights (RR-01, RR-02), and will not abandon a resident.

definitions.definition: The end of a resident's stay at the facility, whether the resident leaves by choice or the facility requires the resident to leave.
A move of the resident to another setting, such as a hospital, nursing facility or other residence.
The written notice to the resident and representative of the reason for, and date of, a required discharge or transfer, as provided in the Resident Contract.
A policy stated in the contract on holding a resident's bed during a hospital stay and the charges that apply.

procedures: When the Administrator finds that a resident no longer meets criteria or the facility cannot meet the resident's needs (ADM-05), the Administrator documents the facts, the rule or contract basis and the practitioner's input on the Discharge/Transfer Determination form.

The Administrator meets with the resident and representative promptly to explain the reason and discuss options, and invites the resident's practitioner, case manager or family to take part. Language and communication needs are met (RR-07).

The Administrator gives the resident and representative written notice stating the reason, the planned date and the resident's rights, within the period required by the contract. Notice also includes the AHCA and Long-Term Care Ombudsman Program contact information and the Abuse Hotline number, 1-800-962-2873. Where the resident has an LMH or Medicaid case manager, the Administrator also notifies them.

Where a resident or representative disagrees about whether the placement is appropriate, the Administrator follows s. 429.26(8), F.S., keeps the resident in the facility while the process runs unless safety requires immediate action, and documents each step and every contact with AHCA and the practitioner.

The Administrator helps the resident find a suitable place, giving a list of options, sending the needed records (with consent) and arranging a safe transfer. Social work or case management referrals are made where appropriate.

If the resident needs immediate care that the facility cannot provide, staff call 911, send the resident to the hospital under HS-04, and the Administrator tells the representative at once. A later decision not to readmit follows the contract bed-hold policy and this procedure.

Before the resident leaves, a nurse or trained staff member reconciles the resident's medications, sends medications and orders as permitted, and gives the receiving provider a current medication list and care summary (HS-01).
Staff return all resident funds and personal property, and have the resident or representative sign an inventory receipt (RR-04).

The Business Office calculates the final charges and any refund of deposits or prepaid fees following the contract refund policy and s. 429.24, F.S., and gives the resident or representative an itemized final statement within [NUMBER] days.
For a voluntary discharge, the resident or representative gives notice as stated in the contract. The Administrator confirms it in writing, completes a discharge checkout and processes refunds.
For a death, HS-08 applies in place of this policy.
The Administrator enters the admission or discharge date, destination and reason in the admission/discharge log required by Rule 59A-36.015, and completes any required report (REC-02).
The Administrator completes the discharge summary, closes and secures the resident record, and retains it as required (REC-01).
The Administrator reviews all involuntary discharges each quarter for quality assurance, to check notice, resident rights and any trends (GOV-03).

responsibilities.duty: Makes and documents discharge decisions, gives timely notice, follows s. 429.26(8) for disputes, and completes the log.
Reconcile medications and prepare the care summary for transfer.
Calculates final charges, refunds and deposits as required by contract and s. 429.24.
Take part in planning and receive notice and records.

documentation: Discharge/Transfer Determination form
Written transfer notice and proof of delivery
Records of disagreement process under s. 429.26(8)
Medication reconciliation and care summary
Property and funds inventory receipt
Itemized final statement and refund record
Admission/discharge log entry
Discharge summary

policies.title: Medication Management, Storage and Disposal
policies.applies_to: Administrator, licensed nurses, all staff who handle, store, assist with or dispose of resident medications
policies.purpose: To make sure resident medications are stored securely, labeled and ordered correctly, tracked, and disposed of on time, and that any central-storage rule is disclosed to residents before admission.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] stores all medications in a locked area or container and permits access only to authorized staff and, for their own medications, to residents who are assessed as able to self-administer. Medications are kept in their original, properly labeled containers and are given or assisted with only as ordered by a licensed practitioner. A medication observation record is kept for every resident who receives assistance with, or administration of, medications. Discontinued, expired and unneeded medications are removed from use and disposed of within the timelines set by Rule 59A-36.008, F.A.C. If staff perform any laboratory test, the facility holds the required CLIA certificate first. This policy meets Rule 59A-36.008(6)(b)6., F.A.C. (official checklist item: central storage of medication, with the policy provided to the resident before admission as required in Rule 59A-36.006, F.A.C.). Where the facility's house rules require central storage of medications, that requirement is written in the house rules and the admission package, and it is given to the resident or representative before admission. The Administrator records the facility's central-storage decision (required, not required, or required with documented exceptions) in the house rules. The admission package states the decision either way, so the reviewer and residents can see it.

definitions.definition: A facility rule that resident medications are kept in one facility-controlled locked location (medication room, cart or cabinet) rather than in the resident's room.
The written record kept for each resident receiving medication assistance or administration, showing each dose, date, time and the staff member who assisted or administered.
A resident taking his or her own medication independently, with or without staff assistance as allowed by Rule 59A-36.008.
The federal Clinical Laboratory Improvement Amendments certificate required before facility staff perform any laboratory test.

procedures: The Administrator decides whether the facility requires central storage of medications and writes the decision, and any exceptions, into the house rules (see RR-01) and the admission package (see ADM-02).

Before admission, the admissions staff member gives the resident or representative the central-storage statement in writing, reviews it, and obtains a signature or dated initials. The signed page is filed in the resident record.
Medications are stored in a locked medication room, cabinet, cart or resident-room locked container. Keys or codes are held only by authorized staff identified by the Administrator in writing.
Medications requiring refrigeration are kept in a locked or access-controlled refrigerator, separated from food, and the refrigerator temperature is checked and logged daily by the shift lead.

Before accepting any medication, the staff member checks that the container label shows the resident's name, drug name, strength, directions, prescriber, date and pharmacy, and compares it with the current practitioner's order. Discrepancies are held and reported to the Administrator or nurse the same shift.

Medications are not relabeled, transferred between containers, or altered by staff. Pill organizers are filled only as permitted by Rule 59A-36.008, and only by the resident, a family member, a licensed nurse, or others as allowed by the rule. Staff do not fill organizers without that authority.
Orders are kept in the resident record. Any change of order is documented, and the label or pharmacy supply is updated before the changed medication is given.

A medication observation record is started on the day of admission or medication start for each resident who receives assistance or administration, and is completed at the time of each dose. Refusals, omissions and errors are documented the same shift.
Medication errors or unexplained shortages are reported at once to the Administrator, who notifies the practitioner and resident representative as needed and records the event under SAF-02.
Over-the-counter or stock medications are kept only as permitted by Rule 59A-36.008, are labeled and ordered for the individual resident, and are stored in the locked area.

If any staff member performs a laboratory test (for example, a fingerstick glucose), the Administrator confirms the facility has the CLIA certificate before the test is done, keeps the certificate on file, and posts or produces it for the surveyor.
Once a month, the Administrator or designee audits storage areas for locks, expired items, discontinued medications, labels and MOR completeness, and records the audit and corrective actions.

Discontinued, expired and unneeded medications are separated, labeled and secured. They are returned or disposed of within the timelines in Rule 59A-36.008, and the date, drug, quantity, method and two staff signatures are recorded.

Medications of a resident who dies or is discharged are handled under the disposal and return provisions of Rule 59A-36.008. The release to the resident, representative or discharge destination is documented and signed.
Medication management findings are reported to the quality assurance committee (see GOV-03).

responsibilities.duty: Sets the central-storage decision, controls keys and authorized access, holds the CLIA certificate when required, and reviews monthly audits.
Verifies orders, supervises storage and disposal, and addresses errors and discrepancies.
Store, assist with and record medications according to this policy and complete the MOR at each dose.
Give and document the central-storage disclosure before admission.

documentation: Signed central-storage disclosure (resident record)
Medication observation records
Practitioner orders
Medication disposal log with two signatures
Refrigerator temperature log
Monthly storage audits
CLIA certificate, if applicable
Medication error reports

policies.title: Medication Administration and Staff Authorization
policies.applies_to: Administrator, licensed nurses, and unlicensed staff who assist with medications
policies.purpose: To define who may assist with self-administration or administer medications, what training and consent are needed, and how infection control is maintained during medication tasks.
policies.policy: Only licensed nurses acting within their scope of practice administer medications at [AGENCY NAME]. Unlicensed staff may only assist residents with self-administration, and only after completing the required 6-hour medication assistance training, with a training certificate from a registered nurse or a pharmacist on file, and only when the resident or representative has given written informed consent. Each assisting staff member completes 2 hours of medication assistance continuing education annually. Pill organizers and self-administration follow Rule 59A-36.008, F.A.C. This policy meets Rule 59A-36.008(3)(h), F.A.C.: all trained staff must adhere to the facility's infection control policy and procedures (SAF-13) when assisting with the self-administration of medication. Staff follow standard precautions and the bloodborne pathogens standard, 29 CFR 1910.1030, when handling medications, sharps or body fluids.

definitions.definition: Helping a resident who can direct their own care take medications that the resident could take without help, such as reminding, opening containers, reading labels, or handing the medication to the resident, as permitted by Rule 59A-36.008.
Directly giving or applying a medication to a resident; performed by licensed nurses only.
The resident's or representative's written agreement to staff assistance with self-administration, after explanation of what staff will and will not do.

procedures: The Administrator keeps a roster of staff authorized to assist with medications, listing the date each completed the 6-hour medication assistance course and the date of the annual 2-hour CE.

No unlicensed staff member assists with medications until the Administrator has verified and filed the training certificate issued by a registered nurse or pharmacist, as required by Rule 59A-36.011 and s. 429.52, F.S.
Before the first dose, the nurse or Administrator reviews the resident's assessed ability to self-administer (see ADM-03) and explains in plain language what assistance staff may provide.
The resident or representative signs a written informed consent for assistance with self-administration. The consent is filed in the resident record before staff assist.

Medications that require administration, such as injections or other tasks beyond assistance, are performed only by a licensed nurse on a practitioner's order. Unlicensed staff are directed to refuse and to notify the nurse or Administrator immediately.

Before each assisted dose, staff wash or sanitize hands, confirm the resident's identity, and compare the label with the medication observation record. Staff use gloves and other protective equipment as required by SAF-13.
Staff observe the resident taking the medication, never leave doses unattended, and never crush, split or mix medications unless ordered or labeled to allow it.
Staff record each dose on the medication observation record at the time of assistance. Refusals and omissions are documented the same shift.
If the resident refuses, vomits, has a reaction, or the medication is unavailable, staff notify the nurse or Administrator immediately, who contacts the practitioner and documents the contact.

Sharps, contaminated materials and spilled medications are handled and disposed of under SAF-13 and the bloodborne pathogens standard. Needlestick or exposure events are reported to the Administrator the same shift.
Pill organizers are used only as permitted by Rule 59A-36.008. The person who fills them signs and dates the organizer log, and the contents are checked against current orders weekly.

A resident assessed as able to self-administer keeps medications as allowed by house rules and HS-01, in a locked container in the room, and staff check at least monthly that the resident continues to manage them safely.
The Administrator observes each assisting staff member's technique at least annually and after any medication error, and documents retraining.
The Administrator confirms the annual 2-hour CE for each assisting staff member is complete. Any staff member whose CE is overdue is removed from medication assistance until it is completed.

responsibilities.duty: Verifies training certificates and CE, maintains the authorized-staff roster, and removes non-compliant staff from medication duties.
Administers medications, trains and supervises assisting staff as designated, and evaluates self-administration ability.
Assist only within their training, obtain consent confirmation, follow infection control, and document each dose.
Provide written informed consent and report concerns about medications.

documentation: 6-hour medication assistance course certificates (RN or pharmacist)
Annual 2-hour CE records
Authorized-staff roster
Written informed consent for assistance
Medication observation records
Pill organizer log
Annual technique observation and retraining records
Exposure incident reports

policies.title: Nursing Services and Delegation (LNS)
policies.applies_to: Administrator, nurses, and staff in a facility holding or applying for a Limited Nursing Services (LNS) license
policies.purpose: To set out how [AGENCY NAME] provides limited nursing services only under an LNS license, with a nurse available, a practitioner's order, monthly assessments and progress notes.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] provides nursing services beyond the standard assisted living scope only if it holds a specialty Limited Nursing Services (LNS) license issued under s. 429.07, F.S., and Rule 59A-36.022, F.A.C. The facility employs or contracts with a nurse who is available as needed. Every nursing service is provided on a practitioner's order. A nurse assesses each resident receiving nursing services monthly and keeps nursing progress notes. The nursing services offered, and their costs, are described in the admission package. Unlicensed staff do not perform nursing tasks. Staff training follows Rule 59A-36.011, F.A.C.

definitions.definition: A specialty license that permits the facility to provide limited nursing services in addition to personal and supportive services (s. 429.07, F.S.).
A written or documented order from a licensed practitioner who is authorized to order the nursing service.
A dated, signed entry by the nurse recording the service provided and the resident's status.

procedures: The Administrator confirms the LNS specialty license is issued and posted before any limited nursing service is offered or provided (see GOV-02).

The Administrator contracts with or employs a nurse and documents the nurse's license, contact information and how the nurse is available as needed, including after hours. Staff keep the contact information on every shift.
The admission package lists each nursing service the facility provides and its cost. The admissions staff member reviews the list with the resident or representative before admission (see ADM-02).
Before a nursing service starts, the nurse obtains the practitioner's order and files it in the resident record. No service is provided without an order.
The nurse completes an initial nursing assessment before services start and adds the nursing service to the service plan (see ADM-04).
The nurse performs and documents a nursing assessment for every resident receiving nursing services at least monthly, and more often when the resident's condition changes.
The nurse writes a progress note each time a nursing service is provided and at least monthly, recording the service, the resident's response and any practitioner contact.
The nurse decides which tasks may be assisted by trained unlicensed staff under the facility's training and scope rules. Tasks requiring nursing judgment or licensure are done only by the nurse.

Unlicensed staff receive the training required by Rule 59A-36.011 and any task-specific instruction from the nurse. The nurse records the instruction and the Administrator files it in the personnel record.
When a resident's condition changes, the nurse notifies the practitioner and the resident's representative and follows HS-04. The nurse recommends reassessment as needed (see ADM-03).
If a resident needs nursing services the facility is not licensed or staffed to provide, the Administrator follows ADM-05 and ADM-06 for retention and discharge.
The Administrator reviews LNS records quarterly, as part of quality assurance, to confirm each service has an order, a monthly assessment and progress notes (see GOV-03).

responsibilities.duty: Holds and posts the LNS license, contracts for the nurse, ensures nurse availability, and reviews LNS records.
Obtains orders, assesses monthly, documents progress notes, directs staff on permitted tasks, and notifies practitioners.
Do only the tasks they are trained and permitted to do and report changes to the nurse.

documentation: LNS license
Nurse employment or contract and availability schedule
Practitioner orders
Monthly nursing assessments
Nursing progress notes
Admission package nursing-services list and costs
Nurse instruction records for staff

policies.title: Change of Condition, Physician Notification and Hospital Transfer
policies.applies_to: All care staff, nurses, Administrator
policies.purpose: To make sure significant changes in a resident's condition are recognized, recorded, reported to the practitioner and representative, and that transfers to hospital are safe and well documented.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] supervises residents and keeps a written record of significant changes in condition as required by Rule 59A-36.007(1), F.A.C. Staff report any change at once to the Administrator or nurse. The facility notifies the resident's representative and practitioner, arranges health care and transportation as required by Rule 59A-36.007(3), F.A.C., and ensures a new medical examination is completed after a significant change as required by Rule 59A-36.006, F.A.C. In an emergency, staff call 911 first. When a resident is transferred, staff send the Do Not Resuscitate Order (DNRO) form if one exists, with current records.

definitions.definition: A change in the resident's physical, mental or functional condition that is not temporary and affects the resident's care needs, such as new inability to bear weight, new confusion, a new pressure sore, or a need for services the facility must reassess.
The Florida Do Not Resuscitate Order form, usually printed on yellow paper, signed by the physician, that emergency personnel honor.

procedures: Any staff member who notices a change in condition (for example, a fall, new confusion, refusal of food or fluids, fever, pain, a skin change, or a change in mobility) reports it immediately to the shift lead, nurse or Administrator.
In an emergency or if life is at risk, staff call 911 immediately, begin first aid or CPR as trained unless a valid DNRO applies (see RR-05), and then notify the Administrator.

The nurse or designee checks the resident, records vital signs if staff are trained and equipped to do so, and decides whether to notify the practitioner immediately or at the next business day. When in doubt the practitioner is called immediately.
Staff contact the resident's practitioner and record the date, time, person contacted, information given and orders received.
Staff notify the resident's representative or designated contact the same shift, and record the time and person spoken to. If no one can be reached, staff keep trying and document each attempt.
Staff write a note of the significant change in the resident record, with date, time, description, actions and who was notified, as required by Rule 59A-36.007(1).
The Administrator arranges needed health care and transportation, including appointments, ambulance or facility transport, as required by Rule 59A-36.007(3), and records the arrangement (see DL-04).

For hospital transfer, staff send with the resident or to the receiving facility: the face sheet, current medication list and medication observation record, recent practitioner orders, DNRO form if one exists, advance directive information, representative contact information, and the name of a staff contact.

A staff member accompanies the resident or follows with personal items, glasses, hearing aids and dentures when feasible, and sends a short written account of the change in condition and any behaviors.
The Administrator or nurse calls the hospital for status updates and keeps the representative informed.
The Administrator logs the incident and notifies the state if the event is reportable (see SAF-02 and REC-02).

When a significant change occurs, the Administrator schedules a reassessment and updates the service plan (see ADM-03 and ADM-04) and confirms that a new medical examination is obtained or updated, as required by Rule 59A-36.006.

On return, the Administrator or nurse reviews the discharge orders, updates the medication list and service plan, and determines whether the resident still meets continued residency criteria, including the bedridden limit of 7 consecutive days. If not, ADM-05 and ADM-06 are followed.
The Administrator reviews change-of-condition and transfer records monthly as part of quality assurance (see GOV-03).

responsibilities.duty: Recognize and report changes immediately and document observations.
Assesses, contacts the practitioner, and directs follow-up.
Ensures notifications, transport, reassessment and examination updates are completed and records are kept.

documentation: Change-of-condition written record
Practitioner and representative notification log
Transfer packet checklist
DNRO form copy
Updated service plan
Incident report where applicable
New medical examination (Form 1823 or practitioner's form)

policies.title: Dementia and Memory Care
policies.applies_to: Administrator, admissions staff, all staff who care for residents with Alzheimer's disease and related disorders (ADRD)
policies.purpose: To make sure residents with Alzheimer's disease and related disorders receive appropriate care, that any special-care advertising is matched by a written description of services, and that staff are trained.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] serves residents with Alzheimer's disease and related disorders only within the limits of its license and its admission and retention criteria (ADM-01, ADM-05). If the facility advertises that it provides special care for individuals with Alzheimer's disease and related disorders, it provides a written description of those special services as required in Section 429.177, F.S., which satisfies Rule 59A-36.006(3)(a)13., F.A.C. (official item: written description of special Alzheimer's services, included in the admission package). Staff who provide direct care to ADRD residents complete the ADRD training required by Rule 59A-36.011, F.A.C. Residents with ADRD are identified for emergency planning (see SAF-09). Advertisements are retained as required by Rule 59A-36.015(1)(h), F.A.C.

definitions.definition: Alzheimer's disease and related disorders, including other forms of dementia.
Any services, environment or programming the facility describes or advertises as specific to ADRD residents.

procedures: Before any marketing is issued, the Administrator decides whether the facility will advertise special care for ADRD and records the decision. If it will not advertise it, no marketing material refers to memory care or dementia-specific services.

If the facility advertises ADRD care, the Administrator prepares a written description of the special services, including staffing and training, activities, environment and safety features, supervision and any additional cost, as required by Section 429.177, F.S.

Admissions staff include the written description in the admission package and give it to the resident or representative before admission (see ADM-02). A signed receipt is filed in the resident record, as required by Rule 59A-36.006(3)(a)13.
The Administrator keeps a copy of each advertisement, brochure and web posting for the period required by Rule 59A-36.015(1)(h) and checks that each is consistent with the written description.
During pre-admission screening (ADM-01), the nurse or Administrator documents cognition, wandering history, behaviors and supervision needs, and decides whether the facility can meet them safely.

The Administrator ensures every staff member who provides direct care to ADRD residents completes the ADRD training required by Rule 59A-36.011 within the required time frames, and files certificates in the personnel record (see STF-03).
The service plan for each resident with ADRD addresses cognition, communication, behavior, daily routines, wandering risk, nutrition, and meaningful activities (see ADM-04 and DL-02).
Staff use person-centered, non-physical approaches to distressing behaviors. Restraints are not used except as allowed under SAF-04.
Residents at risk of wandering are identified, and the elopement risk is added to the service plan and the missing-resident procedures (see SAF-03).

The Administrator keeps a current list of residents with ADRD and of residents needing mobility assistance, used for the emergency management plan and evacuation, and updates it when residents are admitted, discharged or change status (see SAF-05 and SAF-09).
Staff report any behavior change, increased agitation or new safety risk to the nurse or Administrator, who follows HS-04.
If a resident's behaviors or needs exceed what the facility can safely provide, the Administrator follows ADM-05 and ADM-06.
The Administrator reviews ADRD services, training and advertising annually and during quality assurance reviews (see GOV-03).

responsibilities.duty: Controls advertising, prepares the written description, ensures ADRD training and maintains the ADRD resident list.
Provide the written description before admission and obtain a signed receipt.
Complete ADRD training and apply the service plan and behavior approaches.
Screens cognition and behavior and advises on appropriateness of placement.

documentation: Written description of special Alzheimer's services (Section 429.177, F.S.)
Signed receipt in resident record
Retained advertisements
ADRD training certificates
ADRD resident list for emergency planning
Service plans addressing ADRD needs

policies.title: Falls Prevention and Skin Integrity
policies.applies_to: Administrator, nurses, direct care staff, housekeeping and maintenance staff
policies.purpose: To reduce falls and pressure injuries by identifying risk, using assistive devices safely, documenting events, and meeting admission and continued-residency limits for pressure sores.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] identifies residents at risk of falls and skin breakdown, plans prevention in the service plan, and responds promptly to any fall or skin change. Under Rule 59A-36.006, F.A.C., the facility does not admit a resident who has a stage 3 or stage 4 pressure sore, and a resident with a stage 2 pressure sore is retained only as that rule allows. A resident who is bedridden may not remain beyond 7 consecutive days unless covered by the hospice exception. Assistive devices are used in accordance with Rule 59A-36.007(9), F.A.C. Every fall is documented as an incident, and significant skin changes are reported to the practitioner.

definitions.definition: Localized injury to skin or underlying tissue from pressure, staged 1 to 4 by depth.
Equipment such as a walker, cane, wheelchair, grab bar or bed rail that helps a resident move or stay safe.
An unplanned descent to the floor or other lower surface, with or without injury.

procedures: During pre-admission screening and the admission assessment, the nurse or Administrator documents fall history, mobility, balance, vision, medication effects, continence, and skin condition, including any pressure sore and its stage (see ADM-01 and ADM-03).
A person with a stage 3 or 4 pressure sore is not admitted. The admissions staff member records the reason and refers the person to appropriate providers (see ADM-01).

Fall and skin-care interventions are written into the service plan, such as supervision level, assistance with transfers and toileting, footwear, lighting, repositioning and nutrition and hydration support (see ADM-04).

Assistive devices are checked on arrival and routinely for fit and condition and are used as directed by the practitioner or therapist, in accordance with Rule 59A-36.007(9). Staff do not use bed rails or other devices as a restraint (see SAF-04).
Maintenance staff inspect hallways, bathrooms, grab bars, and lighting monthly and remove trip hazards promptly. Housekeeping reports and cleans spills immediately (see DL-03).
Care staff check resident skin during bathing and personal care. They report any redness, open area, blister or discoloration to the nurse or Administrator the same shift.
After any fall, staff do not move a resident who may be injured. They call 911 if needed, check for injury, make the resident comfortable and notify the nurse or Administrator immediately.
The Administrator or nurse notifies the practitioner and the resident's representative of every fall with injury and of any pattern of falls, and documents the contacts (see HS-04).
Staff complete an incident report for every fall the same shift, and the Administrator reviews it within one business day (see SAF-02). Reportable events are forwarded as required under REC-02.
Within 72 hours of a fall, the nurse or Administrator reviews the circumstances and updates the service plan with new interventions.

The nurse reports a new skin change, including any stage 1 or stage 2 area, to the practitioner promptly and records the order, treatment and follow-up. Treatment is delivered only by staff licensed to do so, or by a home health or hospice provider under HS-07.

The Administrator monitors each resident with a stage 2 condition to confirm that services are available as Rule 59A-36.006 requires. If the condition worsens to stage 3 or 4, or the resident is bedridden beyond 7 consecutive days outside hospice, the Administrator starts ADM-05 and ADM-06.
The Administrator tracks falls and skin events monthly by resident, time and location, and brings trends to the quality assurance committee (see GOV-03).

responsibilities.duty: Ensures screening limits are applied, reviews incidents, and acts on trends and continued-residency limits.
Assesses skin and fall risk, notifies the practitioner and updates interventions.
Provide assistance, check skin, report changes and respond to falls.
Keep the environment and equipment safe.

documentation: Admission skin and fall-risk assessment
Service plan interventions
Fall incident reports
Practitioner and representative notification records
Skin-change records and orders
Monthly fall and skin trend log
Assistive device inspection records

policies.title: Hospice and Home Health Coordination
policies.applies_to: Administrator, nursing staff or contracted nurse, direct care staff, and any hospice, home health or other third-party provider serving a resident of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To make sure residents who are terminally ill or who need home health services receive coordinated, uninterrupted care in the facility. The facility's own responsibilities must stay clear, and the provider's plan of care must be followed, including when a resident has a cardiac or respiratory arrest.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] allows residents to receive hospice and home health services from outside providers of their choice and coordinates with those providers as required by Rule 59A-36.007, F.A.C. The bedridden limit in Rule 59A-36.006, F.A.C. (not bedridden, and a maximum of 7 consecutive days of bedridden status) does not apply to a resident who is receiving hospice services. A terminally ill resident who is enrolled in hospice may be retained under the continued residency criteria of Rule 59A-36.006(4), F.A.C., if the facility, the hospice and the resident or representative agree that the resident's needs can be met and the facility's license allows it. When a resident receives third-party services, [AGENCY NAME] communicates with the provider within 30 days as required by Rule 59A-36.007(6), F.A.C., and keeps the communication current as the resident's condition changes. If a resident on hospice has a cardiac or respiratory arrest, hospice procedures take precedence, and staff honor an executed DH Form 1896 under Rule 59A-36.009, F.A.C. (see RR-05).

definitions.definition: A licensed hospice program that provides palliative and supportive care to a terminally ill resident under a hospice plan of care.

An outside agency or individual, such as a home health agency, hospice or therapy provider, that provides services to a resident in the facility but is not employed by or under contract to the facility.
Unable to change position or transfer without total assistance and confined to bed. The 7-consecutive-day limit in Rule 59A-36.006, F.A.C. does not apply to a resident receiving hospice.
The Florida Do Not Resuscitate Order form that must be executed and in the resident's record for staff to honor a DNRO.

procedures: The Administrator or designee reviews the resident's request for hospice or home health services with the resident or representative, and confirms who will arrange the services. The resident's choice of provider is respected. The facility does not require use of a particular agency.

The Administrator confirms that any arrangement keeps the resident within the facility's license and the continued residency criteria of Rule 59A-36.006, F.A.C. For a terminally ill resident on hospice, the Administrator documents the retention decision under Rule 59A-36.006(4), F.A.C. The decision is made with the hospice, the resident or representative and the resident's practitioner.

For hospice enrollment, the Administrator obtains the hospice agency's name, 24-hour contact number, hospice case manager and plan of care. These are entered in the resident record and on the staff communication sheet.

The Administrator, or the nurse for ECC or LNS residents, meets with the hospice case manager before or at the start of services. They agree in writing on who provides which tasks, such as personal care, medication assistance, comfort measures, equipment and supplies, and after-hours calls. The agreed division of tasks is added to the service plan (see ADM-04).

Within 30 days after third-party services begin, as required by Rule 59A-36.007(6), F.A.C., the facility makes documented contact with each third-party provider.
