It confirms the resident's services and schedule, exchanges current medication and diet information, and shares the facility's contact numbers and emergency procedures. The date and person contacted are recorded in the resident record.

The facility updates each provider whenever the resident has a significant change in condition, hospitalization, fall, medication change or change in care needs. These updates are made the same day when possible and are recorded (see HS-04).

The resident's medications and treatments are reconciled with the hospice or home health medication list at start of services and whenever orders change. Medication handling follows HS-01 and HS-02, including storage of hospice comfort kits in the locked medication area.

At or before the start of hospice, staff check the resident's record to see whether a DH Form 1896 has been executed and note this in the record. Staff do not require a DNRO as a condition of admission or continued stay, and they offer information on advance directives (see RR-05).

The facility posts a care alert sheet at the resident's medication location, or in the record, that says whether a DNRO is in place, the hospice agency's 24-hour number, and the instruction to call hospice first for a change in condition or arrest.

If a hospice resident has a cardiac or respiratory arrest, staff immediately follow the hospice procedures. They call the hospice's 24-hour number. If an executed DH Form 1896 is in the record, they do not begin resuscitation. If no executed form is present, they follow facility emergency procedures and call 911. They notify the Administrator and the resident's representative.

Staff provide comfort-focused care in line with the hospice plan of care. This includes pain and symptom observation, repositioning, mouth care, hydration and nutrition offered as the resident accepts, privacy, and emotional and spiritual support. Staff report any uncontrolled pain or symptoms to hospice at once.

The Administrator arranges for hospice and home health staff to receive access to the building and the resident's room during agreed hours. Staff verify identification of visiting providers and record visit dates in the resident record or visitor log.

For a resident who is bedridden for reasons other than hospice, staff count the consecutive days from the first day. The Administrator reviews continued residency with the practitioner before the 7th consecutive day, and the resident is discharged or transferred under ADM-05 and ADM-06 if criteria are no longer met.

The Administrator reviews each hospice and home health arrangement at least quarterly and whenever the resident's condition changes. The review covers whether the facility can still meet the resident's needs with the provider's services, and the findings are recorded in the resident record.

If the resident or representative revokes hospice, or the provider ends services, the Administrator contacts the practitioner and reviews the service plan and continued residency criteria within [NUMBER] business days.

responsibilities.duty: Makes retention decisions, ensures third-party communication within 30 days, assigns staff to coordinate with providers, and reviews arrangements at least quarterly.

responsibilities.role: Nurse (LNS/ECC) or designated health care staff
responsibilities.duty: Exchanges clinical information with hospice and home health, reconciles medications, and updates the service plan.
Deliver comfort care and personal care as assigned, observe and report changes, and follow the alert sheet and hospice arrest procedures.
Provides the services in its plan of care and responds to the facility's calls 24 hours a day.

documentation: Hospice or home health agreement, plan of care and contact information in the resident record
Documented third-party communication within 30 days of the start of services, and later updates
Retention decision for terminally ill resident on hospice
Record of whether DH Form 1896 is executed
Service plan showing task division between facility and provider
Quarterly arrangement review notes

policies.title: Death of a Resident
policies.applies_to: Administrator, all direct care and nursing staff, and administrative staff responsible for resident records at [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To make sure that when a resident dies, staff respond appropriately, the resident's DNRO is honored where applicable, the right people are notified, the resident is treated with dignity, and the facility's records are completed and kept as required.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] treats each death with dignity and respect for the resident's wishes and family. Staff honor an executed DH Form 1896 under Rule 59A-36.009, F.A.C. and follow hospice procedures where the resident is on hospice. The Administrator promptly notifies the resident's representative and the resident's health care practitioner. The admission/discharge log is updated to reflect the death, and the resident's records are retained at the facility's physical address for the period required by Rule 59A-36.015, F.A.C. (resident contracts for 5 years; other resident records for 2 years after the resident's departure).

definitions.definition: A death of a resident with a known terminal condition, usually under hospice care, who has an executed DNRO or a plan of care for end of life.
A death with no hospice or terminal diagnosis, or where the cause is unclear or there are signs of injury, abuse, neglect or foul play.
The family member, guardian, health care surrogate or other person designated in the resident's record to be notified and to act for the resident.

procedures: Staff who find a resident unresponsive, not breathing or without a pulse immediately check the resident's record for an executed DH Form 1896 and the resident's hospice status. They call the Administrator or the on-call manager.

If an executed DH Form 1896 is in the record, staff honor it and do not begin resuscitation. If the resident is on hospice, staff call the hospice's 24-hour number and follow the hospice procedures, which take precedence (see HS-07). Staff stay with the resident until a licensed practitioner or hospice nurse arrives.
If no executed DH Form 1896 is in the record and the resident is not on hospice, staff trained in CPR start CPR and call 911 immediately. They continue until emergency personnel take over.

If the death appears unexpected, unattended or suspicious, staff call 911 and leave the room and the resident's belongings undisturbed except for emergency care. The Administrator contacts law enforcement and the medical examiner as the situation requires and follows SAF-01 and SAF-02 if abuse, neglect or injury is suspected.

The Administrator or designee notifies the resident's representative by phone as soon as possible, ideally within one hour of death or of the time the representative is found. If the representative cannot be reached, the Administrator makes further attempts and records each attempt. Notification is given in person or by phone, not by text or email.

The Administrator or designee notifies the resident's attending practitioner, and the hospice if applicable, so the death can be pronounced and the certificate completed according to Florida law. The time of notification and name of the person notified are recorded.

Staff treat the resident with dignity. They provide privacy, keep the room door closed, and handle the resident gently. They inform other residents who knew the resident in a sensitive manner, and the Administrator arranges support or counseling as needed.

The Administrator arranges release of the body to the funeral home or other entity chosen by the representative or named in the resident's pre-arrangements. The release is recorded with the date, time, funeral home name and the staff member releasing the body.

A staff member or the Administrator inventories the resident's personal property and any funds held for the resident with a second staff member present, and records the inventory (see RR-04). Property and funds are released only to the representative or legal personal representative, who signs a receipt. If it is unclear to whom the property belongs, the Administrator seeks legal advice before release.

The Administrator removes the resident's medications from active use. Medications are handled under HS-01 (storage and disposal), with disposal witnessed by two staff and recorded. Hospice-provided medications are disposed of as the hospice directs.
On the day of death, the Administrator or records staff updates the admission/discharge log with the resident's name, date and the reason for departure as death.

The Administrator reviews the death for any reporting obligation. A death that occurs with an unusual circumstance, injury, accident, abuse or neglect allegation is reported as required (see SAF-02 and REC-02).

The nurse or designated staff writes a final record entry. It states the date, time and circumstances of death, the status of the DH Form 1896, who was called and when, the persons notified, and the release of the body. Entries are factual and signed.
The Administrator refunds any prepaid fees in accordance with the admission agreement and the refund terms in RR-03, and in line with Florida law.

The resident's record is closed and kept at the facility's physical address, readily available for inspection. The resident contract is kept for 5 years, and other resident records are kept for 2 years after the date of death, as required by Rule 59A-36.015, F.A.C.

Within [NUMBER] days, the Administrator reviews each death, especially unexpected deaths, to identify whether the care or response needs improvement, and includes the findings in the quality assurance review (see GOV-03).

responsibilities.duty: Directs the response, ensures notifications, controls release of the body and property, and ensures the log and records are updated and retained.
Check the DNRO and hospice status, start CPR or honor the DNRO as applicable, call the right people, protect the resident's dignity and complete their entries.

responsibilities.role: Nurse or designated health care staff
responsibilities.duty: Coordinate with the practitioner and hospice and complete clinical documentation.
Update the admission/discharge log, close the record and apply the retention schedule.

documentation: Final record entry describing the death and the DH Form 1896 status
Record of notifications to the representative, practitioner, hospice and others, with times
Admission/discharge log updated with the date of death
Property and funds inventory and release receipts
Medication disposal record
Release-of-body record
Retention of resident contract for 5 years and other resident records for 2 years after the resident's departure

policies.title: Extended Congregate Care: Aging in Place, Residency Criteria, Services and Staffing
policies.applies_to: Administrator, ECC supervisor, nurse, direct care staff and admissions staff at [AGENCY NAME], which holds an Extended Congregate Care (ECC) specialty license. This policy applies only while the facility holds an ECC license.
policies.purpose: To set out the written policies and procedures that an ECC-licensed facility must have under Rule 59A-36.021, F.A.C., so that residents can age in place and receive additional personal, supportive and nursing services without having to move out, while the facility maintains adequate staffing and honors resident choice.
policies.policy:
[AGENCY NAME] holds an Extended Congregate Care specialty license under s. 429.07, F.S. and provides ECC services only as described in this policy. This policy meets Rule 59A-36.021(2)(a), F.A.C. (aging in place, with specific written policies and procedures); Rule 59A-36.021(2)(b), F.A.C. (residency criteria developed in accordance with the admission and discharge requirements in subsection (4) and the ECC services in subsection (7)); Rule 59A-36.021(2)(c), F.A.C. (personal and supportive services, how they are provided and the staff positions responsible); Rule 59A-36.021(2)(d), F.A.C. (nursing services and nursing staff); Rule 59A-36.021(2)(e), F.A.C. (unscheduled resident service needs); and Rule 59A-36.021(2)(f), F.A.C. (mediation of room and roommate conflicts). It also meets Rule 59A-36.006(3)(a)12., F.A.C., which requires the admission package to describe ECC residency criteria, additional services and costs, and any limits on where ECC residents may reside. Resident choice under Rule 59A-36.021(2)(g), F.A.C. is addressed in HS-10.

Aging in place [Rule 59A-36.021(2)(a)]: A resident who meets the ECC residency criteria below may remain in the facility as needs increase, so long as the facility can safely meet the resident's needs with ECC services and its staffing, and the resident does not require services the facility cannot provide (see ADM-05). The facility does not discharge a resident solely because the resident needs ECC services. It reviews continued residency under Rule 59A-36.006, F.A.C. and ADM-05.

Residency criteria [Rule 59A-36.021(2)(b) and Rule 59A-36.006(3)(a)12.]: The facility's ECC residency criteria are those in ADM-01 and ADM-05. These are the admission and continued residency criteria of Rule 59A-36.006, F.A.C., applied together with the ECC services the facility has listed in its license application. A resident is accepted or retained in ECC when assessed needs can be met by the ECC services described below, the resident or representative agrees, and the resident's practitioner has no medical contraindication. The facility describes these criteria, the additional services, the additional costs and any limitations on where ECC residents may reside in the admission package given to each prospective and current resident.

Personal and supportive services [Rule 59A-36.021(2)(c)]: ECC services are provided in addition to the standard ALF services of the admission agreement. The services, who provides them, and the staff's relationship to the facility are listed in Procedure 5.

Nursing services [Rule 59A-36.021(2)(d)]: A nurse is on staff or under contract as listed in Procedure 6. The nurse conducts monthly nursing assessments of ECC residents and the service plan of each ECC resident is reviewed at least quarterly.

Unscheduled needs [Rule 59A-36.021(2)(e)]: The facility identifies the types of unscheduled needs ECC residents may have and the resources used to meet them, as set out in Procedure 10.

Room and roommate conflicts [Rule 59A-36.021(2)(f)]: The facility mediates conflicts among residents over choice of room, apartment or roommate as set out in Procedure 11.

Staffing: [AGENCY NAME] provides adequate awake staff at all hours to meet the needs of ECC residents (see STF-01), and staff receive ECC training under Rule 59A-36.011, F.A.C.

definitions.definition: A specialty ALF license under s. 429.07, F.S. that allows the facility to provide additional personal, supportive and nursing services so that residents can age in place.
A resident's ability to remain in the facility as care needs increase, with ECC services, instead of moving to a higher level of care, as long as the resident meets residency criteria.
The staff member designated by the Administrator to supervise ECC services and staff on a day-to-day basis.
A care need that arises without notice, outside the service plan, such as a sudden change in condition, an acute illness or additional help with activities of daily living.

procedures: Before the facility provides any ECC service, the Administrator confirms that the ECC specialty license is current and that this policy and the ECC training plan are in effect. If the ECC license lapses or is revoked, no resident receives ECC services until the license is reinstated.

Admissions staff apply the residency criteria in ADM-01 and ADM-05 to every prospective ECC resident. Staff use the resident's health assessment and the face-to-face medical examination (AHCA Form 1823 or the practitioner's equivalent form) to decide whether the resident's needs can be met by the ECC services below. The decision is recorded and signed by the Administrator.

Admissions staff give every prospective resident, at or before admission, the written ECC description in the admission package. It lists the ECC residency criteria, the additional personal, supportive and nursing services, the additional costs, and any limits on where ECC residents may live in the facility. The resident or representative signs a receipt, which goes in the record (see ADM-02 and RR-03).

For a current resident whose needs increase, the Administrator and nurse hold a reassessment (see ADM-03). If the resident meets the ECC residency criteria, the Administrator explains the ECC services and costs in writing, obtains the resident's consent, updates the service plan (see ADM-04) and updates the admission agreement as needed.

The ECC personal and supportive services are: [LIST ECC PERSONAL AND SUPPORTIVE SERVICES, e.g., total or extensive help with bathing, dressing, toileting, transferring and eating, additional supervision, and specialized diets]. Each service is delivered by the staff position named here. [POSITION TITLE] employed by the facility provides [SERVICES]; [POSITION TITLE] under contract with [CONTRACTOR NAME] provides [SERVICES]. Each position's relationship to the facility (employee or contractor) is recorded in the staffing plan.

The ECC nursing services are: [LIST NURSING SERVICES, e.g., monthly nursing assessments, nursing observation, health monitoring and ordered nursing treatments within the scope of the nurse's license]. The nurse is [NURSE NAME, LICENSE TYPE (RN or LPN)], who works for the facility as [staff or contractor]. The nurse's general working hours are [HOURS], and the nurse is supervised by [ADMINISTRATOR NAME or ECC SUPERVISOR]. Where the nurse is an LPN, the LPN works under the supervision of an RN or other licensed practitioner as the law requires. The nurse's license status, duties, general working hours and supervision are documented in the staffing plan, and the plan is updated whenever the nurse changes.

The nurse completes a nursing assessment of each ECC resident at least monthly and records the findings in the resident record. The nurse reports any change in condition to the practitioner and the Administrator (see HS-04).

The service plan of each ECC resident is reviewed at least quarterly by the nurse, the Administrator or ECC supervisor, and the resident or representative. It is revised after any significant change (see ADM-04 and HS-10). Each review is dated and signed.

The Administrator schedules enough awake staff, at all hours, to meet ECC residents' needs, including at night. The Administrator reviews the schedule each week against the ECC residents' assessed needs and adds staff when needs increase (see STF-01). The staffing sheet shows which staff are awake and on duty at each hour.

Unscheduled service needs: The Administrator and nurse identify the unscheduled needs likely to arise for current ECC residents (for example, acute illness, increased confusion, falls, sudden need for added help with activities of daily living or after-hours nursing questions). For each, the plan names the resource that will meet the need. The resources are: the on-call nurse at [PHONE]; the on-call manager at [PHONE]; the resident's practitioner; hospice or home health provider; additional staff called in from [STAFF POOL OR AGENCY]; and 911 for emergencies. The on-call list is posted in the staff area and reviewed monthly.

Room and roommate conflicts: If residents have a conflict over choice of room, apartment or roommate, the Administrator or ECC supervisor meets separately with each resident, and with each resident's representative if requested, within 3 business days. The Administrator then holds a joint meeting where appropriate and offers options such as a different room, a different roommate, or schedule changes. The resident's wishes are given priority where possible. The conflict, the options offered and the result are recorded. A resident who remains dissatisfied may use the grievance procedure (see RR-02).

Training: Before ECC services begin, and within the time required by Rule 59A-36.011, F.A.C., the Administrator and ECC supervisor complete 4 hours of ECC training and then complete 4 hours of continuing education every 2 years. Direct care staff who provide ECC services complete 2 hours of ECC training. The Administrator keeps certificates in the personnel file (see STF-03 and STF-05).

The Administrator reviews the ECC program at least quarterly. The review covers the number of ECC residents, staffing against the assessed needs, completion of the monthly nursing assessments and quarterly service plan reviews, resident and family feedback, and any transfer or discharge of an ECC resident. Findings are included in the quality assurance review (see GOV-03).

responsibilities.duty: Maintains the ECC license, approves ECC admissions and retention decisions, ensures adequate awake staffing, keeps the staffing plan current and completes ECC training.
Supervises ECC services and staff, helps mediate room and roommate conflicts and makes sure the quarterly service plan reviews are held.
Completes monthly nursing assessments, provides nursing services within license scope, reports changes in condition and takes part in service plan reviews.
Provide ECC personal and supportive services under the service plan, complete 2 hours of ECC training and report changes in residents' needs.
Provide the ECC description, costs and room limits in the admission package and record the receipt.

documentation: Current ECC specialty license
Written ECC residency criteria and the ECC section of the admission package, with the resident's signed receipt
Staffing plan listing ECC personal and supportive service positions and nursing positions, license status, duties, hours and supervision
Monthly nursing assessments
Quarterly service plan review records
Awake staff schedules for all hours
On-call and unscheduled-needs resource list
Room and roommate conflict mediation records
ECC training certificates (4 hours Administrator and ECC supervisor plus 4 hours CE every 2 years; 2 hours direct care staff)

policies.title: Extended Congregate Care: Resident Choice and Participation
policies.applies_to: Administrator, ECC supervisor, nurse, activities staff, direct care staff, and drivers or transportation staff at [AGENCY NAME] while the facility holds an ECC license
policies.purpose: To make sure residents who receive Extended Congregate Care services are involved in decisions about their own care and daily life, and are given opportunities and encouragement to make personal choices, as required by Rule 59A-36.021(2)(g), F.A.C.
policies.policy: This policy meets Rule 59A-36.021(2)(g), F.A.C. [AGENCY NAME] involves ECC residents in decisions that concern them and provides opportunities and encouragement for each resident to make personal choices and decisions. If a resident needs help to make a choice or decision, the facility consults a family member or other resident representative. At a minimum, each ECC resident is given the choice whether: (1) to take part in developing, implementing, reviewing and revising the resident's service plan [Rule 59A-36.021(2)(g)1.]; (2) to remain in the same room in the facility, except that a current resident who transfers into ECC services may be required to move to the part of the facility licensed for ECC if only part of the facility is licensed [Rule 59A-36.021(2)(g)2.]; (3) to select among social and leisure activities [Rule 59A-36.021(2)(g)3.]; (4) to take part in activities in the community, with the facility arranging transportation to such activities, at a minimum, if the resident requests it [Rule 59A-36.021(2)(g)4.]; and (5) to give input on the adoption and amendment of facility policies and procedures [Rule 59A-36.021(2)(g)5.].

definitions.definition: A decision by the resident about daily life and care, such as the resident's routine, room, activities, outings and participation in service planning.
A family member, guardian, health care surrogate or other person designated to be consulted when a resident needs help to make choices or decisions.
The part of the facility licensed for ECC, if only part of the facility holds the ECC license.

procedures: At admission to ECC, and again whenever a resident begins receiving ECC services, the Administrator or ECC supervisor explains the resident's choices in plain language. The explanation covers the five choices listed in this policy. The resident or representative signs an acknowledgment that goes in the record.

The nurse or ECC supervisor invites each ECC resident to take part in developing the service plan. The resident is asked about his or her preferences, routines and goals, and the plan is written to reflect them (see ADM-04). The resident's signature, or the representative's signature if applicable, shows participation. Where the resident declines to take part, the refusal is recorded.

Service plan implementation, review and revision: The resident is invited to each quarterly service plan review (see HS-09) and to any review after a significant change. The nurse or ECC supervisor discusses what is working, what has changed and any requested changes. Changes are made when they are consistent with the resident's safety and assessed needs, and the resident's input is noted.

Where a resident has difficulty making choices because of cognitive or other limitation, staff use simple explanations, visual aids or additional time. If the resident still needs help, staff consult a family member or the resident's representative and record who was consulted, when and what was decided. The resident is still involved as far as possible.

Same room: The facility honors each resident's choice to remain in the same room. The facility does not move a resident to another room because the resident begins ECC services, except that if only part of the facility is licensed for ECC, a resident who is transferring into ECC services from another part of the facility may be required to move to the licensed section. In that case, the Administrator explains the reason in writing before the move, offers the resident a choice of available rooms in the ECC section, and records the discussion. Room moves for other reasons follow the admission agreement and RR-01.

Activities: Activities staff offer ECC residents a monthly activity calendar and ask each resident about interests in an individual conversation at least [FREQUENCY, e.g., quarterly]. Residents choose which social and leisure activities they join, and no resident is required to attend (see DL-02). Staff record each resident's choices and any activities requested that the facility does not currently offer, and the Administrator reviews these requests monthly.

Community activities: A resident who wants to take part in activities in the community, such as religious services, shopping, outings, family events or clubs, tells staff or the Administrator. At a minimum, the facility arranges transportation to the activity when the resident requests it, within [NUMBER] days' notice, and the arrangement is recorded (see DL-04). The facility explains any limits on transportation distance, cost or timing in advance and works with the resident to find an alternative. Staff do not refuse a request merely because it is inconvenient.

Input on policies: The Administrator tells ECC residents and their representatives, at least [FREQUENCY, e.g., annually] and whenever a policy that affects residents is being adopted or changed, how they can give input. This is done at a resident meeting, by a suggestion box or by individual comment. The Administrator records residents' comments, considers them before the policy is adopted or amended, and tells residents what was decided (see RR-01 and GOV-02).

Staff encourage each ECC resident daily to make personal choices, for example about wake-up and bedtimes, meals and clothing, within the limits of safety, the service plan and the rights of other residents. Staff do not make decisions for a resident who can decide.

Staff who see that a resident's choice is being overridden, or who receive a complaint about it, report it to the Administrator the same day. The Administrator investigates, corrects the problem and records the outcome. A resident who is unhappy about how choice was handled may use the grievance procedure (see RR-02).

The ECC supervisor audits a sample of ECC resident records at least quarterly to confirm that choices and participation are documented, including participation in service planning, the room choice, activity selections, community activity requests and policy input. Gaps are corrected within [NUMBER] days and reported in the quality assurance review (see GOV-03).
All staff who provide ECC services are trained in this policy during orientation and annually (see STF-03).

responsibilities.duty: Ensures residents are told of and can exercise their choices, approves arrangements for transport and room issues, collects resident input on policies and reviews records.
Involves residents in developing, reviewing and revising the service plan, consults representatives where needed and documents participation.
Offer a choice of social and leisure activities and record resident selections and requests.
Arrange transportation to community activities when residents request it.
Support and encourage resident choices daily and report any concerns about choice to the Administrator.

documentation: Signed acknowledgment of ECC resident choices
Service plan showing resident participation and quarterly reviews
Record of consultation with family or representative when the resident needs help to decide
Room choice and any required move within an ECC-licensed part of the facility, with explanation
Activity selection and request records
Community activity transportation requests and arrangements
Resident input on policies and facility responses
Quarterly record audit results

policies.title: Limited Mental Health Residents
policies.applies_to: Administrator, admissions staff, direct care staff with direct contact with residents who have mental health needs, and any mental health provider working with [AGENCY NAME]. This policy applies only while the facility holds a Limited Mental Health (LMH) license.
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] admits and serves residents with mental health needs only when properly licensed, trained and organized to do so, and that each such resident has the planning, coordination and respect required by Florida law.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] does not admit or retain a mental health resident unless the facility holds a Limited Mental Health license under s. 429.075, F.S. and Rule 59A-36.020, F.A.C. The facility holds a standard ALF license and has no uncorrected violations that would bar an LMH license. There is no extra AHCA fee for the LMH license. The Administrator and each staff member who has direct contact with mental health residents completes 6 hours of DCF-approved LMH training within 6 months and then 3 hours of continuing education every 2 years, as required for LMH facilities under Rule 59A-36.011, F.A.C. For each mental health resident, the facility keeps a community living support plan and a cooperative agreement with the resident's mental health care provider, as required by Rule 59A-36.020, F.A.C. Mental health residents have the same rights as all residents (see RR-01).

definitions.definition: A specialty license that allows an ALF to admit and serve residents who have a mental health diagnosis, in addition to the facility's standard license.

A resident who has a mental health diagnosis and is eligible for or receiving services as defined in Florida law and Rule 59A-36.020, F.A.C. The Administrator confirms eligibility with the mental health provider.

A written plan developed with the mental health resident that describes the resident's goals and the supports needed to live successfully in the facility and community, and that identifies the staff responsible.
A written agreement between the facility and the mental health provider or case manager serving the resident that sets out how the two will coordinate care and communicate.

procedures: Before admitting any mental health resident, the Administrator confirms that the facility holds a current LMH designation on its standard license, as required by s. 429.075, F.S. If it does not, the facility does not admit the resident and refers the resident to a licensed facility. Staff may not provide LMH services without the license.
The Administrator checks that the facility has no uncorrected violations that would affect the LMH license, and reviews any new survey findings within [NUMBER] business days of receipt.

Admissions staff screen each applicant under ADM-01, including a review of the mental health diagnosis, the medication list, behavior history, current providers and the supports the person needs. Staff apply the same admission and retention criteria as for other residents. The Administrator decides whether the facility can meet the person's needs, and records the decision.

Before or at admission, the Administrator identifies the mental health provider or case manager serving the resident and obtains the resident's written consent to share information (see RR-06). The facility obtains a copy of the provider's treatment recommendations and emergency contacts.

The Administrator signs a cooperative agreement with the resident's mental health provider for each resident. The agreement states how the provider and the facility will share information, who to call about changes in behavior or condition, how appointments will be coordinated and who responds in a crisis. The agreement is kept in the resident record, and a copy goes to the provider.

Within [NUMBER] days of admission, the Administrator or designated staff develops a community living support plan with the resident, the resident's representative if the resident wishes, and the mental health provider. The plan lists the resident's goals, needed supports, community resources, daily living skills, activities and a crisis plan. The resident signs the plan, and a copy is given to the resident.

The Administrator reviews each community living support plan at least [FREQUENCY, e.g., every 6 months] and after any significant change in the resident's condition, hospitalization or behavior. The review involves the resident and the provider, and changes are recorded and signed.

Medications: Mental health residents' medications are stored, assisted with and recorded under HS-01 and HS-02. Staff observe for side effects and for refusal, and report these to the practitioner and the mental health provider the same day.

Training: The Administrator ensures that within 6 months of hire or of assuming LMH duties, the Administrator and every staff member with direct contact with mental health residents complete 6 hours of LMH training approved by DCF, and then 3 hours of continuing education every 2 years. Certificates are placed in personnel files (see STF-03 and STF-05). Staff with no completed training do not work alone with mental health residents until trained, where practicable.

Staff treat mental health residents with dignity and respect, support their rights and choices, and do not use threats, punishment or unnecessary restraint. Restraint and restrictive practices are governed by SAF-04.

Crisis response: Staff who see a mental health resident in crisis, such as suicidal statements, self-harm, severe agitation or danger to others, stay with the resident if safe, remove hazards, call the Administrator or on-call manager and the resident's mental health provider, and call 911 if there is imminent danger. They record the event, and an incident report is completed (see SAF-02 and HS-04).

The Administrator notifies the mental health provider and the resident's representative of a hospitalization, discharge or transfer, and coordinates follow-up care. Discharge follows ADM-05 and ADM-06.

The Administrator reviews the LMH program at least annually. The review covers admissions and discharges of mental health residents, training status, current cooperative agreements and community living support plans, and resident feedback. Results go to the quality assurance review (see GOV-03).

responsibilities.duty: Maintains the LMH license status, decides on admission and retention of mental health residents, signs cooperative agreements, ensures community living support plans, and ensures staff training.
Screen applicants, confirm the LMH license before admission and collect provider information and consent.
Complete LMH training, carry out the community living support plan, observe and report changes and follow crisis procedures.
Provides treatment, takes part in the cooperative agreement and plan, and responds to the facility's concerns.

documentation: Current license showing LMH designation
Admission screening decision for each mental health resident
Cooperative agreement for each mental health resident
Community living support plan for each mental health resident, with reviews
Signed consent to share information
Crisis and incident reports
LMH training certificates (6 hours within 6 months, 3 hours CE every 2 years)

policies.title: Abuse, Neglect and Exploitation Prevention and Reporting
policies.applies_to: All employees, contractors, volunteers and students at [AGENCY NAME], and the Administrator in particular
policies.purpose: To protect residents from abuse, neglect, exploitation and mistreatment, to make sure every concern is reported to the Florida Abuse Hotline immediately, and to protect those who report in good faith.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] has zero tolerance for abuse, neglect and exploitation of residents. Each resident has the right to be free from mistreatment, as set out in the Resident Bill of Rights, s. 429.28, F.S. Every staff member must report known or suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation of a resident to the Florida Abuse Hotline at 1-800-962-2873. The Administrator will make sure the number is posted where residents, families and staff can see it. Staff are trained in resident rights and abuse reporting within 30 days of hire (1 hour), and all staff complete Level 2 background screening before having any resident contact. [AGENCY NAME] will never retaliate against, or allow retaliation against, anyone who makes a good-faith report or complaint.

definitions.definition: Any willful act or threatened act that causes or is likely to cause physical, sexual or psychological harm, including hitting, rough handling, name-calling, humiliation, threats, isolation and unlawful restraint.
Failure or omission to provide the care, supervision, food, medication, hygiene or services a resident needs to maintain physical and mental health.
Improper use of a resident's funds, property or resources for the benefit of someone other than the resident, including theft, coercion, fraud and misuse of authority.
The statewide DCF hotline, 1-800-962-2873, that receives reports of abuse, neglect and exploitation of vulnerable adults, available 24 hours a day.
Fingerprint-based criminal history screening required by Florida law for ALF staff before they have contact with residents (see STF-02).

procedures: Prevention: The Administrator ensures each person who will have resident contact completes Level 2 background screening and receives an eligible result before any resident contact, and that the result is filed in the personnel record (see STF-02). Anyone with a disqualifying result is not allowed resident contact unless a valid exemption has been granted.
Orientation: Every new employee completes the 2-hour pre-service orientation before resident contact, which includes these reporting duties (see STF-03).

Training: Within 30 days of hire, each staff member completes at least 1 hour of training in resident rights and the prevention and reporting of abuse, neglect and exploitation, as required by Rule 59A-36.011, F.A.C. Staff repeat this training at least annually as part of in-service training. Attendance records and certificates are kept in the personnel file (see STF-05).

Posting: The Administrator posts the Florida Abuse Hotline number, 1-800-962-2873, together with the facility's grievance procedure and other required complaint numbers, in a visible location in the facility, in large print. The Administrator checks the postings monthly and records the check (see RR-01 and RR-02).

Recognizing: Staff watch for signs of abuse, neglect and exploitation, including unexplained injuries, bruises or burns, fear of a person, withdrawal, weight loss, poor hygiene, missing items or money, unusual financial activity, and statements by the resident.

Immediate protection: A staff member who sees or suspects abuse, neglect or exploitation first makes sure the resident is safe. They separate the resident from the alleged abuser if possible, call 911 for any emergency or crime, give first aid and call the practitioner for injuries (see HS-04).

Reporting: The staff member who suspects or knows of abuse, neglect or exploitation reports immediately to the Florida Abuse Hotline at 1-800-962-2873, by phone, and does not wait for approval from a supervisor. The staff member also notifies the Administrator as soon as possible, unless the Administrator is the alleged offender. In that case the staff member reports directly to the Hotline and to [GOVERNING BODY CONTACT]. Reporting to the Administrator does not replace the duty to report to the Hotline. [Confirm statutory reporting details before publication.]

The Administrator, or the staff member making the report, writes down the Hotline report date and time, the person who took the report and any report or intake number given. This is recorded in the incident file and kept separately from the resident record.

Staff suspected of involvement are removed from resident contact immediately, and the Administrator decides whether to suspend them pending the outcome of the investigation. Staff do not question or confront the resident or the alleged abuser in a way that could affect an investigation.

Preservation: Staff preserve evidence by not cleaning or discarding clothing, bedding or items involved, and by writing factual statements. The Administrator cooperates fully with the Hotline, law enforcement, AHCA, the Long-Term Care Ombudsman and any investigator, and gives them access to residents, records and staff.

The Administrator notifies the resident's representative promptly of the incident and of the report, unless the representative is the suspected abuser, and then notifies the resident's practitioner if needed. The notification is documented.

The Administrator completes an incident report (see SAF-02) and starts a facility review of the event within 24 hours. The review looks at the cause, any care or supervision failure, steps to prevent recurrence and any staff discipline. Findings go to the quality assurance and risk management process (see GOV-03).

Non-retaliation: No one may retaliate against a staff member, resident, family member or volunteer who reports in good faith, files a complaint or takes part in an investigation. Retaliation includes firing, discipline, schedule changes, threats, transfer or discharge of a resident, and harassment. A staff member who retaliates is subject to discipline, up to dismissal. Anyone who believes retaliation has occurred reports it to the Administrator or to the Hotline.
Failure to report: A staff member who knows or suspects abuse, neglect or exploitation and does not report it is subject to discipline up to dismissal, and may face consequences under Florida law.

Residents may report concerns at any time to any staff member, the Administrator, the Ombudsman or the Hotline. Staff help residents who want to make a report, including helping them with a phone and privacy (see RR-02).
The Administrator reviews all abuse, neglect and exploitation reports and outcomes at least quarterly and reviews this policy at least annually (see GOV-02).

responsibilities.duty: Protect residents, report known or suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation to the Florida Abuse Hotline immediately, notify the Administrator, preserve evidence and cooperate with investigations.
Ensures Level 2 screening and training, posts the Hotline number, ensures reports are made, protects residents and reporters, starts the internal review and prevents retaliation.
Receives reports involving the Administrator and oversees corrective action.

documentation: Level 2 screening results in personnel files
Orientation and abuse-reporting training records (1 hour within 30 days of hire) and annual in-service records
Posted Hotline number check log
Hotline report log with date, time and reference number
Incident reports and internal review findings
Notification to the resident's representative
Records of corrective action and any discipline

policies.title: Incident and Accident Reporting
policies.applies_to: All staff, contracted service providers and volunteers of [AGENCY NAME]; all residents
policies.purpose: To make sure every incident, accident and significant change involving a resident is responded to, documented, communicated to the right people, and reported to AHCA, the Abuse Hotline and other authorities within the required time, and that the facility learns from each event.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] documents every incident or accident involving a resident, staff member or visitor in writing. Staff supervise residents and keep a written record of significant changes in a resident's condition, as required by Rule 59A-36.007, F.A.C. Every incident involving a resident is recorded in that resident's record. The resident's health care practitioner and the resident's representative are notified promptly. Adverse incidents are reported to AHCA under s. 429.23, F.S., within the timeline set by that statute and AHCA's reporting instructions. The Administrator verifies the current timeline and reporting method at least once a year and whenever AHCA changes its instructions, and records the verification date on the Incident Reporting Procedure sheet kept with the incident forms. Suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation is also reported to the Florida Abuse Hotline at 1-800-962-2873 under SAF-01. Evacuation reporting is separate and is handled under SAF-07, which requires a report within 6 hours as provided in Rule 59A-36.019(4), F.A.C. Records are kept at the facility's physical address and are available to surveyors, as required by Rule 59A-36.015, F.A.C. No staff member will be retaliated against for reporting an incident in good faith.

definitions.definition: Any unplanned event that affects or could affect the health, safety or rights of a resident, including falls, injuries, medication errors, elopement or missing resident, choking, resident-to-resident altercations, unexplained injuries, fires, property damage, and unusual occurrences.

An event of the kind defined in s. 429.23, F.S., that must be reported to AHCA. It includes events resulting in or risking death, serious injury, fracture or dislocation, or transfer to acute care because of the event, and any abuse, neglect, exploitation or elopement the statute covers. The Administrator decides reportability with reference to the statute, not this summary.

A change in a resident's physical, mental or functional condition that is a departure from the resident's usual status and that requires a written record, practitioner contact or reassessment (see HS-04 and ADM-03).
The person designated in the admission agreement or by law to receive notices and act for the resident.

procedures: The staff member who sees or learns of an incident first makes sure the resident is safe, gives or calls for first aid, and calls 911 in an emergency. Resident safety comes before paperwork.
The staff member tells the supervisor on duty immediately and the Administrator or designee as soon as possible, and no later than the end of the shift for non-emergency incidents.

The staff member who witnessed the incident completes the facility Incident Report before the end of the shift. The report records the resident's name, date and time, location, what happened (facts only), witnesses, injuries or symptoms, immediate actions taken, and the people notified.

The supervisor or a staff member authorized under HS-03 checks the resident for injury and records the check in the resident's progress notes. Unwitnessed falls and head injuries are monitored and documented as directed by the practitioner or the facility's policy under HS-06.

The supervisor notifies the resident's health care practitioner promptly and records the date, time, person reached and instructions received. If no one can be reached, the supervisor keeps trying and records each attempt.

The supervisor notifies the resident's representative promptly, and the same day for any injury, transfer, or event likely to concern the family. The notification is recorded with the date, time and name of the person told. The Administrator ensures notification of other persons the resident has designated.
The Administrator or designee reviews each incident report within one business day, classifies the event, and decides whether it is an adverse incident under s. 429.23, F.S.

For a reportable adverse incident, the Administrator or designee submits the report to AHCA within the timeline set by s. 429.23, F.S., by the method AHCA directs. Any follow-up or final report required by AHCA is submitted by the due date. The submission confirmation is filed with the incident report.

If the event involves suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation, staff call the Florida Abuse Hotline at 1-800-962-2873 immediately, as described in SAF-01. The Administrator does not delay a hotline report to complete an internal review.

If an incident involves a death, SAF-08's counterpart HS-08 applies. If it involves an elopement, SAF-03 applies. If it involves a medication error, HS-01 and HS-02 apply. If it involves a fire, SAF-12 applies. Reporting under this policy is done in addition to those policies.

The incident is entered in the resident's record (progress notes, with the incident report referenced or filed in the record), and the resident's service plan is reviewed under ADM-04 for changes needed to prevent recurrence. A significant change in condition is recorded in writing and the resident is reassessed under ADM-03 as needed.
The Administrator records every incident in the facility Incident Log, which shows the date, resident, type of event, notifications made, any report made to AHCA or other agencies, and the outcome.

The Administrator reviews the Incident Log at least monthly, looks for patterns by resident, time, location and staff, and takes corrective action. Findings are given to the quality assurance and risk management process under GOV-03.
Staff receive training on this policy at orientation and on adverse incidents and emergency procedures during in-service training under STF-03, as required by Rule 59A-36.011, F.A.C.
Incident reports and logs are retained and kept at the facility's physical address for the periods required in REC-01, and are produced for AHCA surveyors on request.

responsibilities.duty: Secure resident safety, report immediately, and complete the incident report before the end of the shift.
Assess the resident, notify the practitioner and representative, and brief the Administrator.
Classify incidents, submit AHCA and Hotline reports, maintain the Incident Log, verify current reporting timelines, and review trends.
Update the service plan and reassess the resident after an incident.
Receive summaries of incident trends through quality assurance.

documentation: Incident Report form signed and dated by the reporting staff member and the Administrator
Resident progress note describing the event, assessment, and notifications
Record of practitioner and representative notification
Facility Incident Log
Copy of AHCA adverse incident submission and confirmation, and any follow-up report
Abuse Hotline report confirmation number, if applicable
Annual verification of reporting timelines under s. 429.23, F.S.

policies.title: Elopement and Missing Resident
policies.applies_to: All staff, volunteers and contracted providers; all residents, especially residents identified as at risk of elopement
policies.purpose: To prevent residents from leaving the facility unsupervised when this is unsafe, to identify residents at risk, and to locate any missing resident quickly using a trained, rehearsed search and notification procedure.
policies.policy: This policy meets Rule 59A-36.006(3)(a)14., F.A.C. — the facility's resident elopement response policies and procedures. [AGENCY NAME] follows the elopement standards in Rule 59A-36.007(7), F.A.C. Residents at risk of elopement are identified at pre-admission screening, at assessment, and whenever their condition changes, and their service plan includes specific prevention measures. A copy of this elopement response policy is given to every resident or representative in the admission package (ADM-02). All staff are trained on the elopement response procedures within 30 days of hire and must demonstrate competency, and elopement is also an in-service training topic under Rule 59A-36.011, F.A.C. Elopement drills are conducted and documented under Rule 59A-36.007(7)(c), F.A.C., at the frequency set in s. 429.41(1)(k), F.S. The Administrator confirms that frequency each year and records it in the facility's drill calendar. A resident who cannot be located is treated as a medical emergency. The search begins at once and law enforcement is called without delay when required by this policy.

definitions.definition: An occurrence in which a resident leaves the facility or its grounds without the knowledge or supervision of staff, in a manner that places the resident at risk, or when the resident's absence cannot be accounted for.
A resident whose whereabouts are not known and who has not been found after a quick check of his or her room and the usual places.
A resident who has a history of elopement or wandering, has a cognitive impairment, expresses a wish to leave or go 'home', or whose assessment shows exit-seeking behavior.
A scheduled simulated missing-resident exercise in which staff carry out the search and notification steps, which is evaluated and documented.

procedures: At pre-admission screening (ADM-01) and at admission assessment (ADM-03), the Administrator or designee reviews each applicant for elopement history, wandering, exit-seeking behavior and cognitive status, and records the finding in the record.

For each resident found to be at risk, the service plan (ADM-04) lists specific interventions, such as increased checks, escort when outdoors, door alarms or a wearable alert device if the resident is not restrained by it, activity engagement, and review of the resident's routine. Staff apply these interventions every shift. Any restriction must respect SAF-04 and RR-01.

The Administrator keeps a current Elopement Risk List and a current photograph and physical description of each at-risk resident in a place that is quickly accessible to staff on all shifts but protected under RR-06. The list is updated at each service plan review and whenever a resident's condition changes.

Staff check exit doors, alarms and the perimeter fence or gates daily, and the maintenance log (DL-03) shows the date and result of each check. Any defect is repaired or compensated for with added supervision at once.

Staff take a head count at the start of every shift and after meals and activities, and the supervisor confirms at-risk residents' locations at least once every hour or at the interval written in the service plan.

When a resident cannot be found, the first staff member to notice calls out the code word [ELOPEMENT CODE WORD] and notifies the supervisor, who takes charge of the response. Staff must not wait to complete other tasks.

The supervisor assigns staff to search the resident's room, bathrooms, common areas, closets, laundry, kitchen, vehicles, courtyards and all grounds, and assigns one person to watch exits and the front entrance. Another staff member keeps the rest of the residents safe and supervised.

The supervisor calls 911 immediately for an at-risk or cognitively impaired resident, for any resident who needs medications or care to stay safe, or in extreme weather. For any other resident, 911 is called if the resident is not found within 15 minutes of the start of the search. The caller gives the resident's name, description, clothing, photograph availability, medical condition, and last known location and time.

The supervisor notifies the Administrator immediately. The Administrator or designee notifies the resident's representative and health care practitioner as soon as the resident is determined to be missing, and does not wait for the outcome of the search.

The search continues in an expanding pattern, including checking neighbors, nearby roads, water, and the likely destinations of the resident, until law enforcement takes over. Staff provide the police with a photograph and all requested information and remain available to assist.

When the resident is found, staff check for injury, give first aid or call 911, return the resident to the facility, and notify law enforcement, the representative, the practitioner and the Administrator that the resident has been found.

After return, a staff member authorized under HS-03 or the practitioner examines the resident, and a record is made of the resident's condition, including any injury, dehydration or exposure. The resident is monitored closely for the next 72 hours and the results are recorded in progress notes.

The Administrator completes an incident report under SAF-02, determines whether the event is an adverse incident reportable to AHCA under s. 429.23, F.S., and reports it in the required time. If abuse or neglect is suspected, the Hotline is called under SAF-01.

Within 7 days, the Administrator reviews how the resident got out, corrects physical or staffing gaps, and revises the resident's service plan. If the facility can no longer keep the resident safe, the Administrator follows ADM-05 and ADM-06.

All new staff are trained on this policy within 30 days of hire, and staff demonstrate competency by walking through the search and notification steps with the Administrator or a trainer. Competency is recorded in the personnel record (STF-05). Refresher training is held annually as part of in-service training.

The Administrator conducts documented elopement drills at the frequency confirmed under s. 429.41(1)(k), F.S., and Rule 59A-36.007(7)(c), F.A.C., on varied shifts including nights and weekends. Each drill record shows the date, time, shift, staff who took part, time to complete the search, problems found and corrective actions.
The Administrator includes a copy of this policy in each admission package and obtains the resident's or representative's signature acknowledging receipt (ADM-02).

responsibilities.duty: Maintain the Elopement Risk List, ensure training and drills, notify authorities, file reports, and review each event.
Direct the search, call 911 when required, and make the first notifications.
Know at-risk residents, follow interventions, report missing residents at once, and take part in drills.
Check doors, alarms and fencing and repair defects.
Examine and treat the resident on return and advise on service plan changes.

documentation: Elopement risk finding in screening and assessment records
Service plan interventions for at-risk residents
Elopement Risk List with photographs
Daily door, alarm and perimeter check log
Incident report, search record and law enforcement report number
Notification record for representative and practitioner
Elopement drill records with date, shift, participants and results
Staff training and competency records within 30 days of hire
Signed acknowledgement of receipt of this policy in the admission package

policies.title: Restraints and Restrictive Practices
policies.applies_to: All staff, volunteers and contracted providers; all residents
policies.purpose: To protect residents' right to be free from restraint and restrictive practices, to make sure that any restraint used is permitted by Florida rule, ordered, planned for, monitored and documented, and to promote the least restrictive alternatives.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] does not use restraint or seclusion for discipline, punishment, staff convenience or as a substitute for adequate staffing or supervision. Residents have the right to be free from unnecessary restriction, as described in RR-01. If a physical restraint is used at all, it is used only as Rule 59A-36.007(8), F.A.C., allows and as the resident's practitioner has ordered, and only if the resident has a care plan that addresses the restraint. Staff try less restrictive alternatives first, and these are documented. Chemical restraint is not used. A medication is never given to control behavior for staff convenience. Use of an assistive device is governed by Rule 59A-36.007(9), F.A.C., and a device is not used to restrict movement. The facility does not admit or retain a resident whose need for restraint is beyond what the rule permits or what the facility can safely provide (ADM-05).

definitions.definition: Any manual method, or physical or mechanical device, material or equipment attached or adjacent to the resident's body that the resident cannot easily remove and that restricts freedom of movement or normal access to the resident's body.
A psychotropic medication used to discipline a resident or for staff convenience and not required to treat the resident's medical symptoms.
A device such as a walker, wheelchair, cane, grab bar or lap tray used to help the resident function, and which the resident can use or remove at will as the resident's condition allows.
The approach that addresses the safety concern with the smallest limit on the resident's freedom and dignity.

procedures: No staff member may apply any restraint, or lock a resident in a room, without the Administrator's approval and a practitioner's order. In an immediate emergency, staff use only the minimum hold needed to prevent imminent harm and call 911 and the Administrator at once.

Before any restraint is considered, the Administrator or case manager, with the resident's practitioner and representative, identifies the problem, such as falls, wandering or agitation, and tries and documents less restrictive alternatives. Examples are more supervision, a change in the room, lower bed, toileting schedule, medication review, activities, and pain assessment.

If a physical restraint is still thought necessary, the Administrator confirms that its use is allowed under Rule 59A-36.007(8), F.A.C., and ADM-05, and that the resident can safely stay in the facility. If not, the Administrator starts the process under ADM-05 and ADM-06.

A restraint may be used only with a written practitioner order that states the reason, the type of restraint, how long it may be used and the monitoring required. A copy of the order is placed in the resident's record.

The resident or representative is told about the proposed restraint, the risks and the alternatives, and gives informed written consent. The consent is filed in the resident's record, and the resident's rights under RR-01 are respected.

A care plan for the restraint is written before it is used and is part of the service plan (ADM-04). It states the reason, alternatives tried, how and when it is applied and released, skin checks, toileting, nutrition and fluids, repositioning, activity, and the plan to reduce or end use.

Staff check the resident at the frequency stated in the care plan, and record each check. They release the restraint, reposition the resident, offer toileting and fluids, and check skin condition and circulation, and record the times (HS-06).
A restraint is never used in a way that blocks evacuation. Staff are trained to release restraints at once in a fire or other emergency (SAF-12 and SAF-07).

The practitioner and the Administrator review each restraint at least [monthly] and whenever the resident's condition changes. The restraint is ended as soon as it is no longer needed, and the date and reason are recorded.

Bed rails, lap belts, geriatric chairs and similar devices are assessed individually. A device that the resident cannot remove on request is treated as a restraint and all steps in this policy apply. The assessment is recorded in the resident's record (Rule 59A-36.007(9), F.A.C.).
Any injury or adverse effect of a restraint is reported as an incident under SAF-02. Suspected misuse of restraint is reported to the Florida Abuse Hotline at 1-800-962-2873 under SAF-01.
The Administrator keeps a Restraint Log of all residents who have restraints, with the dates of orders, reviews and removal, and reviews it monthly through quality assurance (GOV-03).
All staff are trained at orientation and annually on resident rights, behavior management, de-escalation, and the prohibition of restraint for discipline or convenience (STF-03).
Behavioral symptoms are managed through person-centered approaches described in HS-05 and HS-11 for residents with dementia or mental health needs.

responsibilities.duty: Approve or refuse any restraint, ensure compliance with rule, keep the Restraint Log and review it.
Evaluate the resident, write and renew any order, and review the need regularly.
Write the care plan, assess alternatives and monitor the resident.
Use alternatives, carry out monitoring, release restraints in an emergency and report concerns.
Take part in decisions and give informed consent.

documentation: Record of alternatives tried
Practitioner order
Informed consent from resident or representative
Restraint care plan within the service plan
Monitoring and release records
Periodic review notes
Restraint Log
Staff training records

policies.title: Comprehensive Emergency Management Plan (CEMP): All Hazards, Responsibilities and County Coordination
policies.applies_to: Administrator, all staff and contracted providers; all residents
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] has a written, county-approved Comprehensive Emergency Management Plan that covers all hazards, names responsible staff, coordinates with the county emergency management agency, provides for post-disaster activities, and is understood by every staff member.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] maintains a written Comprehensive Emergency Management Plan (CEMP) on AHCA Form 3180-5006 (Sept 2023), as required by Rule 59A-36.019, F.A.C. This policy meets: Rule 59A-36.019(1)(a), F.A.C. — provision for all hazards; Rule 59A-36.019(1)(f) — identification of and coordination with the county emergency management agency; Rule 59A-36.019(1)(g) — arrangement for post-disaster activities including responding to family inquiries, obtaining medical intervention for residents, transportation, and reporting to the county emergency management agency the number of residents who have been relocated and the place of relocation; Rule 59A-36.019(1)(h) — identification of staff responsible for implementing each part of the plan; and Rule 59A-36.019(3)(a) — all staff are trained in their duties and are responsible for implementing the plan, and new staff are trained on the plan within 30 days of employment. The CEMP is submitted to the county emergency management agency each year, and any significant modification is submitted within 30 days of the change. The county is the final authority on the plan, and the facility makes the changes the county requires. The facility's shelter-in-place and evacuation provisions are in SAF-06 and SAF-07, and its plan for emergency environmental control is in SAF-10.

definitions.definition: The facility's Comprehensive Emergency Management Plan on AHCA Form 3180-5006 (Sept 2023).

Any emergency that threatens the facility or residents, including hurricanes and tropical storms, flooding, tornado, fire, loss of electricity or water, extreme heat, infectious disease outbreak, hazardous materials release, sinkhole, civil disturbance and an active threat.

A change that affects how the plan operates, such as a change of the evacuation destination, transportation provider, shelter agreement, responsible staff, licensed capacity, building or the services provided.
The emergency management agency of the county where the facility is located, which reviews and approves the CEMP.

procedures: The Administrator is responsible for the CEMP. The Administrator completes AHCA Form 3180-5006 (Sept 2023), and the form is kept at the facility, with a copy easy to reach in an emergency and a copy kept off-site.

The plan addresses all hazards under Rule 59A-36.019(1)(a), F.A.C. The Administrator completes a hazard assessment covering at least the hazards listed in the definition, using information from the county emergency management agency, and records the hazards and the specific response for each.

The Administrator identifies the county emergency management agency and records its name, address, phone number and the name of the contact person in the CEMP, as required by Rule 59A-36.019(1)(f), F.A.C. The Administrator keeps these contacts current and checks them at least every quarter.

The Administrator coordinates with the county emergency management agency on evacuation zones, shelter locations, special needs registration, transportation, and local alerting. The Administrator records each contact and any advice received.

The CEMP names, by position and by name, the staff member responsible for each part of the plan, as required by Rule 59A-36.019(1)(h), F.A.C. These include: overall incident commander, communications and family inquiries, resident care and medications, resident records and tracking, transportation and evacuation, supplies, food and water, emergency power and fuel, facility protection, and county reporting. A back-up is named for each role. The assignments are in the Emergency Responsibility Chart in the CEMP, and the chart is updated whenever a person changes.

The post-disaster section of the CEMP, required by Rule 59A-36.019(1)(g), F.A.C., states how the facility will: (a) respond to family and representative inquiries, including a call tree, phone line, website or message board and a daily update schedule; (b) obtain medical intervention for residents by contacting practitioners, EMS, hospitals, hospice and home health agencies; (c) arrange transportation for residents; and (d) report to the county emergency management agency the number of residents who have been relocated and the place of relocation.

After any relocation, the person responsible for county reporting calls the county emergency management agency and gives the number of residents relocated and where they went. The Administrator keeps the resident location record under SAF-07 up to date so that the report is accurate.

The CEMP includes the facility's plans for shelter in place (SAF-06), evacuation (SAF-07), receiving evacuees (SAF-08), residents with Alzheimer's disease or mobility limitations (SAF-09), emergency environmental control (SAF-10) and heat-injury mitigation (SAF-11).

The Administrator submits the CEMP to the county emergency management agency for review each year and keeps proof of the date of submission. The Administrator makes any change the county requires and resubmits it until the county approves it. The county's decision is final.
If a significant modification is made at any time, the Administrator submits the changed plan to the county emergency management agency within 30 days of the change and keeps proof of submission.

The Administrator trains all staff in their duties under the plan, as required by Rule 59A-36.019(3)(a), F.A.C. New employees are trained on the plan within 30 days of the date of hire, and the training is recorded in the personnel record (STF-05). All staff are retrained at least annually and whenever the plan is significantly changed.

Emergency training covers the staff member's assigned role, the hazard-specific response, communication, resident tracking, medication and records handling, and evacuation methods. Staff sign a training roster after each session.

The Administrator tests the plan at least once a year through a drill or tabletop exercise, records the results, and corrects gaps in the CEMP. Results are given to the quality assurance process (GOV-03).

The Administrator gives residents and representatives a summary of the emergency plan at admission and when the plan changes (ADM-02), and provides notices required by Rule 59A-36.025, F.A.C., for emergency environmental control (SAF-10).
A copy of the CEMP, county approval, proof of annual submission and training records are kept at the facility's physical address and are available to AHCA surveyors.

responsibilities.duty: Complete and maintain the CEMP, coordinate with the county, submit annually and within 30 days of significant changes, and train staff.
Carry out the assigned part of the plan as shown on the Emergency Responsibility Chart.
Complete emergency training, including within 30 days of hire, and carry out their duties.
Provide resources needed for emergency preparedness and review the plan each year.
Review and approve the plan as the final authority.

documentation: Completed AHCA Form 3180-5006 (Sept 2023)
Hazard assessment
Emergency Responsibility Chart with named staff and backups
County emergency management contact record
Proof of annual submission and county approval
Proof of submission of significant modifications within 30 days
Staff training rosters and new-hire training records
Annual drill or exercise report
Post-disaster family communication and relocation reports

policies.title: Care of Residents Sheltering in Place
policies.applies_to: Administrator, all staff and contracted providers; all residents who remain in the facility during an emergency
policies.purpose: To make sure residents who remain in the facility during an emergency are kept safe, cared for and supplied, with a prepared building, adequate food, water, staff, emergency equipment and emergency power.
policies.policy: This policy meets Rule 59A-36.019(1)(b), F.A.C. — provision for the care of residents remaining in the facility during an emergency, including pre-disaster or emergency preparation; protecting the facility; supplies; emergency power; food and water; staffing; and emergency equipment. [AGENCY NAME] decides with the county emergency management agency, using the criteria in the CEMP (SAF-05), whether to shelter in place or evacuate. When residents shelter in place, the facility follows the steps below, uses its emergency power and temperature control plan under Rule 59A-36.025, F.A.C. (SAF-10), and takes the heat-injury precautions in SAF-11. If the facility shelters people above its licensed capacity, it keeps a log and files the 48-hour report required by Rule 59A-36.019, F.A.C. (see SAF-08).

definitions.definition: Keeping residents in the facility during an emergency rather than evacuating them.
The alternate power source and fuel the facility maintains under Rule 59A-36.025, F.A.C., to hold safe temperatures and run essential equipment.
Food, water, medications, medical supplies, hygiene items, lighting, communication devices, and other items listed in the CEMP.
A written record of each person sheltered in the facility over licensed capacity, with the time of arrival and departure.

procedures: When a hazard is forecast, the Administrator activates the CEMP, announces the activation to the emergency staff, and decides with the county emergency management agency whether to shelter in place or evacuate. The decision, the time and the reasons are recorded.

Pre-disaster preparation: as soon as a watch or warning is issued, the Administrator reviews the resident list, the Emergency Responsibility Chart, staff availability and the supply inventory. Staff are called in or told to stay at the facility, and each shift's staffing for the emergency is written down.

Protecting the facility: maintenance staff secure or bring in outdoor items, protect windows and doors as the CEMP directs, clear drains, check roof and generator, turn off hazardous utilities when instructed, and photograph the property before the storm. The checklist is signed and filed.

Supplies: before the hazard, the designated staff member counts and restocks emergency supplies. The facility keeps enough water and food, including therapeutic and texture-modified diets, for all residents and staff for at least 96 hours, to match the power-loss planning period in the environmental control plan. Supplies include a flashlight and batteries, first aid kits, incontinence and hygiene supplies, manual can opener, battery or crank radio and charged phones.

Medications: the staff member designated for medication management confirms that each resident has at least a [7]-day supply of medication on hand, refills are requested ahead of the hazard, and medication administration records and practitioner orders are copied for portability (HS-01).

Emergency power: the facility maintains the alternate power source and fuel required by Rule 59A-36.025, F.A.C. Fuel on site must last at least 48 hours for a facility licensed for 16 or fewer beds, and at least 72 hours for a facility licensed for 17 or more beds. The designated staff member tests the generator and checks fuel levels before the hazard, and arranges refueling. A carbon monoxide alarm is installed and tested as required (SAF-10).

Temperature: the facility follows its approved plan to keep the ambient temperature at or below 81°F for 96 hours after loss of power, including use of the designated area of at least 20 net square feet per resident calculated on 80 percent of licensed beds. Staff check and record indoor temperature at least [every 4 hours] during power loss and take heat-injury steps under SAF-11.

Staffing: the Administrator keeps enough staff to meet resident needs and the minimum staffing in STF-01 during the emergency. Staff work in shifts and have rest areas, and the Administrator makes a plan for staff's families as needed.

Resident care: staff keep the daily routine as normal as possible, give medications and meals on schedule, give fluids, assist with toileting and hygiene, and check each resident at least [every 2 hours] and more often for residents with dementia, mobility limits or high-risk conditions (SAF-09). Residents are moved away from windows when high winds are expected.

Emergency equipment: the facility keeps and tests fire extinguishers, oxygen supplies, wheelchairs, evacuation aids, flashlights and radios. Residents on oxygen or electric equipment are identified in advance and a back-up plan is made for each.

Communication: the designated staff member keeps in touch with the county emergency management agency, informs representatives of the facility's status as scheduled in the CEMP, and records every contact. If phone service fails, the back-up communications in the CEMP are used.

If the facility is asked to shelter people from other facilities or the community above its licensed capacity, the Administrator follows SAF-08, keeps a log of each person admitted, and files the 48-hour report required by Rule 59A-36.019, F.A.C.
