If conditions become unsafe, such as a loss of the ability to hold safe temperatures, flooding, structural damage or loss of water, the Administrator consults the county emergency management agency and, if needed, begins evacuation under SAF-07. The change is recorded.

After the hazard, the Administrator inspects the building, checks every resident for injury and condition and records the results, arranges medical care as needed, and begins post-disaster activities under SAF-05, including family communication and county reports.

The Administrator holds a debrief within [7] days after any activation, lists lessons learned, corrects problems and updates the CEMP, and submits significant modifications to the county within 30 days (SAF-05). Incidents during the emergency are reported under SAF-02.

responsibilities.duty: Decide on sheltering in place with the county, direct the response and file reports.
Protect the building, run and fuel emergency power and check temperature controls.
Keep and issue food, water and supplies.
Secure medications, records and care for residents with special needs.
Provide care, check residents and report changes.

documentation: Record of shelter-in-place decision and reasons
Pre-hazard facility protection checklist
Emergency supply inventory
Medication supply and records check
Generator test and fuel log
Temperature and resident check logs
Shelter log and 48-hour report if capacity is exceeded
Communication log
Post-event debrief report

policies.title: Evacuation of Residents
policies.applies_to: Administrator, all staff and contracted providers; all residents who must be evacuated
policies.purpose: To make sure residents who must leave the facility during an emergency are identified, moved safely with their records and medications, sheltered and cared for, tracked at all times, and that evacuation is reported on time.
policies.policy: This policy meets Rule 59A-36.019(1)(c), F.A.C. — provision for the care of residents who must be evacuated from the facility during an emergency, including identification of such residents and transfer of resident records; evacuation transportation; sheltering arrangements; supplies; staffing; emergency equipment; and medications. When evacuation is ordered or decided, [AGENCY NAME] reports the evacuation to the county emergency management agency and to AHCA within 6 hours of the evacuation order, as required by Rule 59A-36.019(4), F.A.C. The facility keeps track of the location of every resident until return. Evacuation steps for residents with Alzheimer's disease or related disorders or with mobility limits are in SAF-09, and fire evacuation is covered in SAF-12.

definitions.definition: The planned movement of residents out of the facility to another location because of an emergency, whether by order of the authorities or by the Administrator's decision.
The location where residents are to be sheltered, as set out in a written agreement or in the county plan.
A portable set of resident identification, face sheet, medication list and records, and emergency contacts that goes with each resident.
A written record showing where each resident is at all times during evacuation and until return.

procedures: The Administrator decides to evacuate when the county orders it, when the CEMP criteria are met, or when the building is unsafe, and records the time of the order or decision. The Administrator activates the evacuation team named in the CEMP (SAF-05).

Within 6 hours of the evacuation order, the Administrator or designee reports the evacuation to the county emergency management agency and to AHCA, as required by Rule 59A-36.019(4), F.A.C. The report gives the facility name, the number of residents, the destination, and a contact number. The time and the person who made each report are recorded.

Identification of residents: the designated staff member prints the current resident roster, notes each resident's mobility, oxygen or equipment use, cognitive status, diet, and need for special transport, and flags residents who need extra help (SAF-09). Each resident wears an ID wristband or tag with name, facility, phone number and diagnoses.

Transfer of records: for every resident, the designated staff member prepares an evacuation packet containing the face sheet, photo, medication administration record and list, practitioner orders, allergies, advance directive or DNR order (RR-05), diet, representative contact, insurance and Medicaid information, and any restraint or behavior plan. The packets travel with the residents, and the facility keeps a copy.

Transportation: the Administrator uses the transportation providers and written agreements listed in the CEMP, confirms their availability as soon as the hazard is forecast, and assigns each resident to a vehicle. Vehicles that carry residents who use wheelchairs or oxygen must be suitable for them. Staff go with the residents in each vehicle.

Sheltering arrangements: the Administrator confirms with the receiving facility or shelter that it expects the residents, and records the contact, address and number it can receive. Residents are not sent to a location that has not accepted them, except a county-designated shelter. A written agreement is kept in the CEMP.

Supplies: staff load enough supplies for the stay, including water, food and special diets, incontinence and hygiene products, bedding, clothes, comfort items, and first aid supplies, for at least the number of days stated in the CEMP.

Medications: the staff member designated for medication management packs each resident's medications in a locked container with labels and the medication administration record, including controlled substances with a count signed by two staff, and refrigerated medications in a cooler. A staff member authorized under HS-02 gives medications during the evacuation and records every dose.

Staffing: the Administrator assigns enough staff to each vehicle and to the receiving site, to keep resident care at least equal to the minimum in STF-01, and plans relief shifts. Staff carry the Emergency Responsibility Chart, contact lists and facility keys.
Emergency equipment: staff take wheelchairs, walkers, oxygen and portable equipment, flashlights, a first aid kit, a battery-powered radio, chargers, and fire safety items needed at the destination.

Tracking: before departure, staff take a head count and mark each resident's vehicle and seat on the resident tracking record. They take another head count on arrival. Any transfer to a hospital or other site is recorded with the time and place. The tracking record is kept up to date for each shift.

Notification: the designated staff member tells each resident's representative where the resident is going, and gives updates as set out in the CEMP. The practitioner is told of any resident whose condition changes. Phone numbers for the receiving site are given to families.

Care during evacuation: staff continue to meet each resident's needs, including meals, fluids, toileting, medications, rest, and supervision for residents with dementia (SAF-09). Staff check residents for signs of heat illness, dehydration and distress. Incidents are reported under SAF-02.

After the evacuation, the Administrator reports to the county emergency management agency the number of residents relocated and the place of relocation, as provided in SAF-05, and updates the report whenever the location or number changes.

Return: when the authorities clear return, the Administrator inspects the building for safety, utilities, supplies and cleanliness. Residents return only when the building can safely meet their needs, and the return is recorded. If the building cannot be reopened, the Administrator arranges relocation, notifies AHCA and representatives, and follows ADM-06 if any resident cannot return.
The Administrator holds a debrief after each evacuation, corrects problems, and updates the CEMP, with significant modifications submitted to the county within 30 days (SAF-05).

responsibilities.duty: Order evacuation, make the 6-hour reports, confirm transportation and shelter, and direct return.
Assign residents to vehicles and confirm vehicle readiness.
Prepare evacuation packets and the resident tracking record.
Pack and secure medications and the medication records.
Prepare residents, travel with them, and give care throughout.

6-hour report to the county emergency management agency and AHCA, with date, time and person reporting
Evacuation roster and special-needs list
Evacuation packet checklist
Transportation and receiving site agreements
Medication transfer and controlled substance count record
Resident tracking record
Family and representative notification log
County relocation report
Return inspection and debrief report

policies.title: Receiving Evacuees from Other Facilities
policies.applies_to: Administrator, designated emergency coordinator, nursing/medication staff, direct care staff, dietary and maintenance staff
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] can safely accept and care for additional residents evacuated from other facilities during an emergency. It sets out how evacuees are identified, how extra staff and supplies are arranged, and how the required report and log are completed.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] will make provision in its Comprehensive Emergency Management Plan (CEMP, AHCA Form 3180-5006) to care for additional residents evacuated to the facility during an emergency. The provision covers identifying those residents, staffing, and supplies. This policy meets Rule 59A-36.019(1)(d), F.A.C. (provision for the care of additional residents who may be evacuated to the facility, including identification of such residents, staffing, and supplies). Before accepting evacuees, the Administrator or designee will determine how many additional residents the facility can safely shelter, based on space, staff, supplies, power and water. If the facility serves as an emergency shelter above licensed capacity, it will keep a log of every evacuee and submit a report to AHCA within 48 hours, as required by Rule 59A-36.019. Evacuees will be treated with the same dignity, rights protections and safety standards as admitted residents. For each evacuee we will record identification, medications and medical conditions on arrival. The facility will not accept evacuees whose needs it cannot safely meet, and will tell the sending facility and county emergency management so the evacuee can be placed elsewhere.

definitions.definition: A resident of another licensed facility (or a person placed by county emergency management) who is brought to [AGENCY NAME] for temporary shelter during an emergency.
Temporary sheltering of evacuees that raises the census above the number of beds on the facility's license, which triggers the 48-hour report and the evacuee log.
The facility's written Comprehensive Emergency Management Plan on AHCA Form 3180-5006, approved by the county emergency management agency.
A running record of each evacuee's name, date and time of arrival and departure, sending facility, contact person, and condition and medication information.

procedures: Pre-emergency planning: each year, when the CEMP is reviewed, the Administrator calculates the number of additional residents the facility can shelter. The calculation considers available floor space, beds or mattresses, bathrooms, staffing, food, water, medication storage and alternate power capacity. The result is written into the CEMP.

The Administrator lists in the CEMP the supplies needed per additional person per day (food, drinking water, incontinence supplies, linens, hygiene items, bedding, medical supplies). The Administrator keeps stock levels or supply agreements to meet that number and records the check dates.

The Administrator lists in the CEMP how additional staff will be obtained (extra shifts, on-call staff, staffing agency or volunteer arrangements). All additional staff who will give care must have completed background screening (STF-02) before working unsupervised.

When a request to receive evacuees arrives from another facility, a family, or county emergency management, the Administrator or designee records the time and caller and checks current capacity, staffing and supplies before agreeing to accept anyone.

Before or on arrival, the designee asks the sending facility for a current resident list, face sheet, medication administration record or medication list, diagnoses, allergies, diet orders, code status or DNRO, mobility and cognitive needs, and emergency contacts. Where this cannot be obtained in advance, the designee collects it at the door.

At arrival, a designated staff member enters each evacuee in the Evacuee Log and puts an identification wristband or tag on each evacuee, including those with dementia. The log records name, date and time of arrival, sending facility, and responsible contact.

A nurse or trained staff member records each evacuee's medications (name, dose, route, time last given, and who supplies them) and known conditions, allergies, and special needs. Medications arriving with evacuees are stored per HS-01 and are given only by staff authorized under HS-02, on the basis of a current order or the sending facility's medication record.

Evacuees with Alzheimer's disease or related disorders, or mobility limitations, are added to the facility's special-assistance list (SAF-09) for the duration of their stay and assigned a staff member for supervision.

The Administrator assigns evacuees to a sleeping area. Residents with dementia, infectious symptoms, or high fall risk are placed where they can be seen most readily. The evacuee area is included in evacuation route and fire safety checks (SAF-12).

Staff give evacuees the same care as residents: meals, therapeutic diets, hydration, toileting and personal care, supervision, and heat-injury monitoring (SAF-11). Any change in condition follows HS-04.

Each shift, the shift supervisor updates the Evacuee Log, counts all evacuees, and reports staffing or supply shortfalls to the Administrator. The Administrator decides whether to stop accepting evacuees.

If the facility is sheltering above licensed capacity, the Administrator submits the required report to AHCA within 48 hours of the first evacuee's arrival, using AHCA's Assisted Living Unit contact ((850) 412-4304, assistedliving@ahca.myflorida.com) or the method AHCA directs. A copy is kept with the log.
The Administrator tells county emergency management of the number of evacuees being sheltered and any unmet needs.

When evacuees leave, staff record the date and time of departure and the person who received them. They return all medications and records to the evacuee or receiving facility with a signed transfer sheet, and note the return in the Evacuee Log.
Within 14 days after the emergency, the Administrator reviews the response with staff, records what worked and what did not, and updates the CEMP and supply lists accordingly (GOV-03).

responsibilities.duty: Sets and approves evacuee capacity, authorizes acceptance, arranges extra staff and supplies, files the 48-hour report with AHCA, and communicates with county emergency management.
Runs the intake process, maintains the Evacuee Log and arrival records, and coordinates with the sending facility.
Records evacuee medications and conditions, secures medications, and gives medications only under HS-01/HS-02.
Supervise and care for evacuees, report condition changes, and assist in keeping the log current.
Prepare space, equipment and food supplies for added residents.

documentation: CEMP section on receiving evacuees (AHCA Form 3180-5006)
Evacuee Log (arrivals, departures, sending facility, contacts)
Evacuee medication and condition records
Capacity, staffing and supply calculation worksheet
Copy of the 48-hour report to AHCA, with date and method of submission
Transfer sheets at departure
Post-event review notes

policies.title: Residents with Alzheimer's/Related Disorders or Mobility Limitations: Specialized Assistance
policies.applies_to: Administrator, nursing and care staff, medication-authorized staff, all direct care staff, emergency coordinator
policies.purpose: To identify residents with Alzheimer's disease or related disorders and residents with mobility limitations who may need specialized assistance, either at the facility or if evacuation is necessary, and to define the assistance each will receive.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] will keep a current written list of residents with Alzheimer's disease or related disorders (ADRD) and residents with mobility limitations, together with the specialized assistance each needs on site and in case of evacuation. This policy meets Rule 59A-36.019(1)(e), F.A.C. (identification of residents with Alzheimer's disease or related disorders, and residents with mobility limitations who may need specialized assistance either at the facility or in case of evacuation). The list is part of the CEMP (AHCA Form 3180-5006). It is updated at least with every CEMP submission (annually, and within 30 days for significant modifications, per Rule 59A-36.019) and after any change in a resident's condition. Staff who may provide this assistance are trained in emergency procedures within 30 days of hire as required by Rule 59A-36.019, and ADRD-trained staff provide care to ADRD residents as required by Rule 59A-36.011. The list is kept confidential under RR-06 but is available immediately to staff on duty and to emergency responders.

definitions.definition: Alzheimer's disease or a related disorder (such as other dementias) that affects memory, judgment, orientation or safety.
A condition that limits a resident's ability to walk, transfer or move safely without help or equipment (for example wheelchair, walker, bed-bound, or one- or two-person assist).
The written, dated roster of ADRD and mobility-limited residents with the assistance each needs, kept with the CEMP and at the staff station.

procedures: At admission and at each reassessment (ADM-03), the nurse or designated staff member checks the resident's diagnoses, assessment and physician's examination for ADRD or any mobility limitation and records the result in the resident record.
The Administrator or designee adds each identified resident to the Specialized Assistance List, recording name, room, diagnosis category (ADRD, mobility, or both), and date entered.

For each listed resident, the nurse or designee writes the on-site assistance needed (for example supervision level, cueing, wandering risk, wheelchair or walker use, transfer method, number of staff needed, oxygen or equipment dependence) and records it on the list and in the service plan (ADM-04).

For each listed resident, the nurse or designee writes the evacuation assistance needed: how the resident will be moved, who is assigned, equipment required (wheelchair, evacuation chair, blankets), whether a calming approach or escort is needed, and transport needs. Where a resident's care is covered in HS-05, the two documents must match.
Each listed resident is assigned a named staff member or position for each shift who is responsible for that resident during an emergency. The assignment is posted on the shift assignment sheet.
Residents with ADRD wear or carry identification as set out in SAF-03 so they can be identified if separated from staff during an emergency.

The Administrator keeps a current copy of the list in the emergency binder and at the staff station, and a copy goes with the resident's medication record and face sheet if the facility evacuates (SAF-07).

The list is updated at least with every CEMP submission and review. The Administrator checks the list against the current census each time before the annual CEMP submission and records the date and name of the checker.

Whenever a resident's condition changes (new diagnosis, fall with injury, decline in mobility, new device, hospital return), the nurse or designee updates the list within one business day and tells the shift supervisor.
New residents are added, and discharged or deceased residents removed, within one business day.

Within 30 days of hire, and before working unsupervised in emergency roles, each employee is trained on the CEMP, including how to find and use the list and the special assistance for each listed resident. Staff caring for ADRD residents also complete the ADRD training in Rule 59A-36.011. Training is recorded in the personnel record (STF-03, STF-05).
The facility includes listed residents in at least one practice of evacuation or sheltering procedures each year and records problems and corrections.

During an emergency, the emergency coordinator checks listed residents first and confirms that each assigned staff member has accounted for his or her resident at each shift change, and during any evacuation (SAF-06, SAF-07).
The Administrator sends the updated list or the information it contains to the county emergency management agency in the form the agency requires, as part of the CEMP submission.

responsibilities.duty: Ensures the list exists, is current, is part of the CEMP, and is reviewed at least with each plan submission.
Identifies residents, defines the on-site and evacuation assistance, and updates the list after changes in condition.
Assigns staff to listed residents each shift and confirms accountability during emergencies.
Know the needs of the listed residents they are assigned to and give the specialized assistance.
Keeps the binder copy, coordinates training and practices, and shares the list with county emergency management and responders.

documentation: Specialized Assistance List with dates of entry, review and update
Resident assessments and service plans showing the same information
Staff assignment sheets for listed residents
Staff emergency-procedure and ADRD training records
Records of practices and corrective actions
CEMP submission and county approval records showing the list was included

policies.title: Emergency Environmental Control: Alternate Power, Fuel and Carbon Monoxide Alarm
policies.applies_to: Administrator, maintenance director, emergency coordinator, all staff on duty during power loss
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] has the alternate power, fuel, maintenance services and carbon monoxide detection needed to keep residents at safe temperatures if primary electrical power is lost.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] will maintain on site an alternate power source (generator or equivalent) and enough fuel to keep ambient air temperatures at or below 81°F for at least 96 hours after the loss of primary electrical power, in the area(s) designated in its approved plan. The policy meets the following items of Rule 59A-36.025, F.A.C.: (1)(a) — alternate power source capable of holding 81°F or lower for a minimum of 96 hours, with the plan naming the area(s) where temperature will be maintained and the systems, equipment and fuel needed to operate them (Rule 59A-36.025(1)(a)1.-3.); (1)(b) — sufficient fuel, safely stored, with fuel source and storage described in the plan; (1)(c) — a contract or arrangement for services to maintain and test the equipment; and (1)(d) — acquisition and maintenance of a carbon monoxide alarm. The designated cooled area provides at least 20 net square feet per resident, calculated on 80% of licensed beds. On-site fuel is at least 48 hours of supply for a facility of 16 or fewer licensed beds, or 72 hours for 17 or more licensed beds; the plan documents how the balance of the 96-hour requirement is met through resupply arrangements. The environmental control plan is submitted before licensure, and proof of county emergency management approval is sent to AHCA within 30 days of approval.

definitions.definition: A generator or equivalent permanently maintained at the facility that can operate the cooling systems and other equipment needed to hold the designated area at or below 81°F during loss of primary power.
The area or areas named in the plan where temperature is maintained at or below 81°F, sized at least 20 net square feet per resident, calculated on 80% of licensed beds.
Usable floor area of the designated space, excluding areas not available for residents to occupy, such as fixed equipment, closets and walls.
The air temperature in the occupied space as measured by a thermometer placed at resident level.

procedures: Before licensure, the Administrator and maintenance director (or qualified engineer or contractor) determine the area(s) of the building where 81°F will be maintained and calculate the net square footage. The area must provide at least 20 net sq ft per resident, calculated on 80% of licensed beds. The calculation and floor plan are kept in the plan.

The contractor or engineer lists the systems and equipment needed to cool that area (air handlers, condensers, fans, lighting, refrigeration, communications, medical equipment) and calculates the electrical load the generator must carry. The plan records generator size, fuel type, and load calculation.

The plan states the fuel source, the amount stored on site, the storage location and safety measures, and the burn rate at the calculated load. On-site fuel must meet the minimum of 48 hours (16 or fewer licensed beds) or 72 hours (17 or more licensed beds). The plan also names the fuel supplier and the arrangement that ensures resupply so operation can continue for 96 hours.

The Administrator signs a written service agreement with a qualified provider for maintenance and testing of the generator and associated equipment, and records the contractor's name, phone, and the service schedule in the plan (Rule 59A-36.025(1)(c)).

Maintenance staff or the contractor run and load-test the generator on the schedule in the service agreement and manufacturer instructions, at least [TESTING FREQUENCY, e.g., monthly run and annual load test]. Each test is logged with date, runtime, fuel level before and after, problems found and repairs made.

Maintenance staff check fuel quantity at least weekly and before any forecasted storm or emergency. They top off fuel when it falls below the minimum required quantity and record the readings on the Fuel Log.

A working carbon monoxide alarm is installed and maintained as the plan describes, in the location(s) required by the Florida Building Code and the plan (including near fuel-burning equipment). Maintenance staff test the alarm at least monthly and replace batteries or the unit according to the manufacturer's instructions. Tests are logged.

Generators and fuel-burning equipment are never operated indoors or in enclosed spaces, and exhaust is directed away from air intakes, doors and windows. Where a portable unit is used, it is placed and operated as the plan shows.

Staff on duty are trained within 30 days of hire in how to start, shift to, and monitor the alternate power source, including who to call if it fails (STF-03). A written start-up checklist is posted at the generator.

The Administrator submits the environmental control plan to the county emergency management agency for approval before licensure (or when a significant change is made to equipment or capacity). The Administrator sends AHCA proof of county approval within 30 days of approval and keeps the confirmation in the file.

Within 5 business days, as required by Rule 59A-36.025, the Administrator gives residents (and representatives) written notice of the facility's emergency environmental control procedures. The notice is timed from county approval or approval of any change, and given to new residents at admission. The date of each notice is recorded.

For facilities with 17 or more licensed beds, maintenance staff also check that the AED on the premises (s. 429.255(3)(a), F.S.) is working and has its battery and pads current. The AED is included in the emergency supply check.

When primary power is lost, the shift supervisor immediately notifies the Administrator, confirms the generator has started, moves residents to the designated cooled area as needed, and begins temperature checks and the heat-injury procedures in SAF-11. Each check is logged.

If the generator fails or fuel runs low, the Administrator contacts the service contractor and fuel supplier, notifies county emergency management, and starts sheltering or evacuation decisions under SAF-06 and SAF-07.
After every outage or test failure, the Administrator reviews performance, corrects deficiencies, updates the plan if needed, and records the review (GOV-03).

responsibilities.duty: Ensures the plan is complete, submitted before licensure, approved by the county, and proof sent to AHCA within 30 days; gives resident notice; keeps contracts current.
Maintains the generator, fuel supply and carbon monoxide alarm; completes tests and logs; coordinates with the service contractor and fuel supplier.
Maintains and tests the alternate power source under the written agreement.
Activates the checklist at power loss, monitors temperature and fuel, and reports to the Administrator.
Know the location and start-up procedure for the alternate power source and report any alarm or failure at once.

documentation: Emergency environmental control plan with floor plan, net sq ft calculation (20 sq ft x 80% of licensed beds), equipment and load list
Generator and fuel specification, fuel supplier and resupply agreement
Generator service and testing contract
Generator test and fuel logs
Carbon monoxide alarm test log
County approval and proof sent to AHCA within 30 days
Dated resident notices (5 business days)
Power-outage temperature logs and post-event reviews

policies.title: Heat-Injury Mitigation During a State of Emergency
policies.applies_to: Administrator, nurse/medication staff, direct care staff, dietary and maintenance staff, shift supervisors
policies.purpose: To protect residents from heat-related injury and dehydration when the facility is occupied during a declared state of emergency, and to make sure the alternate power source can be activated effectively and immediately.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] has written policies and procedures to effectively and immediately activate, operate and maintain the alternate power source and any fuel needed for it, and to care for residents occupying the facility during a declared state of emergency. This policy meets Rule 59A-36.025(5)(a), F.A.C., and describes the methods used to reduce the risk of heat-related injury: (5)(a)1. — use of cooling devices and equipment; (5)(a)2. — use of refrigeration and freezers to produce ice and maintain appropriate temperatures for medicines requiring refrigeration; (5)(a)3. — wellness checks by staff to monitor for signs of dehydration and heat injury; and (5)(a)4. — provision for obtaining medical intervention from emergency services for residents whose life safety is in jeopardy. The written procedures are given to residents in a notice within 5 business days, as required by Rule 59A-36.025.

definitions.definition: An emergency declared by the Governor or a local authority that affects the facility's area.
A face-to-face check by trained staff of a resident for signs of dehydration or heat injury, with the findings recorded.
Illness caused by heat exposure, including heat cramps, heat exhaustion and heat stroke.
A resident who shows signs that life is threatened, such as unresponsiveness, confusion with hot dry skin, very high body temperature, fainting, seizure, or difficulty breathing.

procedures: When a state of emergency is declared for the facility's area, the Administrator reviews this policy and the CEMP with the shift supervisors, confirms the generator and fuel are ready (SAF-10), and records the date and time.

Cooling devices and equipment (5)(a)1.: maintenance staff set up and test the cooling equipment named in the plan (air conditioning on alternate power, portable fans, portable cooling units, cooling towels and cold packs, as the plan specifies). They record the locations and the date tested. Residents are moved into the designated cooled area if the temperature rises above 81°F.

The shift supervisor checks and logs the temperature at resident level in each occupied area at least [TEMPERATURE CHECK INTERVAL, e.g., every 2 hours] and whenever power is lost. If any occupied area is above 81°F, staff move residents to cooler space, open shades or close blinds as appropriate, and tell the Administrator.

Refrigeration and ice (5)(a)2.: before the emergency, dietary staff make and store ice, stock cold drinking water, and keep refrigerator and freezer doors closed as much as possible. During a power outage, the generator's load plan keeps refrigeration running for food and for medications requiring refrigeration.

Medication staff check refrigerated medication storage temperatures at the start of each shift and after any power interruption and log them. If the temperature goes out of range, they follow HS-01 and contact the pharmacist or physician about the usability of the medications.

Wellness checks (5)(a)3.: trained staff check every resident for signs of dehydration and heat injury at least [WELLNESS CHECK INTERVAL, e.g., every 2 hours] during the state of emergency and whenever temperatures are elevated. Residents with ADRD, mobility limits, heart or kidney disease, or on diuretics or psychotropic drugs, and residents who cannot ask for fluids, are checked more often (SAF-09).

Staff look for dry mouth, dark urine or little urine, thirst, flushed or very pale skin, heavy sweating or lack of sweating, dizziness, headache, weakness, cramps, nausea, rapid pulse, new confusion or sleepiness. Each check is recorded on the Wellness Check Log with the time, the staff member's initials and any action.

Staff offer fluids to residents at least [FLUID OFFER INTERVAL, e.g., hourly] unless fluid is restricted by a physician. Residents on restrictions are checked with the nurse or physician, and the guidance is recorded.

Staff encourage light clothing and cool wet cloths, help residents to cooler spaces, and monitor residents who cannot move themselves. They give cold fluids and ice as appropriate and record intake for residents at risk.

Medical intervention (5)(a)4.: when a resident shows signs that life safety is in jeopardy (for example, temperature of 103°F or higher, confusion with hot dry skin, fainting, seizure, unresponsiveness), staff call 911 immediately, start cooling measures and first aid, and notify the Administrator. Staff trained in First Aid/CPR stay with the resident until emergency services arrive.

For less urgent signs of heat illness, staff contact the resident's physician or the facility nurse for orders and follow HS-04. Any resident who is transferred has the transfer recorded and the representative notified.
The Administrator keeps current phone numbers for 911, county emergency management, the generator contractor, fuel supplier and pharmacy at the staff station.

If the alternate power source fails, or the cooled area cannot be kept at or below 81°F, the Administrator contacts county emergency management and decides whether to shelter in place elsewhere or evacuate (SAF-06, SAF-07).

Within 5 business days of county approval of the plan or of any change in these procedures, the Administrator gives written notice of the heat-injury procedures to residents and representatives, and records the date. New residents get the notice at admission.

All staff are trained on these procedures in preservice orientation or emergency-procedures training (STF-03). Within 14 days after an emergency, the Administrator reviews the logs and the response and corrects any problems (GOV-03).

responsibilities.duty: Ensures procedures are in place, readiness is confirmed when a state of emergency is declared, notices are given, and problems are corrected.
Assigns wellness checks, monitors temperature logs, and activates 911 or the physician when needed.
Monitor medication refrigeration, advise on fluid restrictions, and assess residents with signs of heat illness.
Complete wellness checks, offer fluids, move residents to cooler space, and report signs of heat injury at once.
Operate cooling equipment and refrigeration and make ice and stock water.

documentation: Written heat-injury mitigation procedures (this policy and CEMP section)
Temperature logs, refrigerator and freezer temperature logs
Wellness Check Logs and fluid intake records
Emergency call and transfer records
Dated resident notices
Staff training records
Post-event review notes

policies.title: Fire Safety, Evacuation and Drills
policies.applies_to: Administrator, maintenance director, all staff, shift supervisors, volunteers
policies.purpose: To protect residents, staff and visitors from fire by meeting the fire safety standards that apply to assisted living facilities, keeping the building and equipment in safe condition, and making sure staff know how to respond and evacuate.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] will comply with the Florida Building Code and the fire safety standards in chapter 69A-40, F.A.C. (Uniform Fire Safety Standards), as referenced by Rule 59A-36.014, F.A.C. The local fire authority or the State Fire Marshal inspects the facility for fire safety under Rule 59A-36.005, F.A.C.; the county health department inspects sanitation, food hygiene and biomedical waste; and AHCA inspects all other matters. Copies of the annual fire and sanitation inspection reports are sent to the AHCA Central Office within 30 calendar days (Rule 59A-36.004). The facility does not use uninspected space for residents without prior approval from the AHCA Field Office, and does not change licensed capacity without prior AHCA Central Office approval (Rule 59A-36.004). The facility keeps master keys to all resident bedrooms so staff can enter in an emergency (Rule 59A-36.014). If licensed for 17 or more beds, the facility keeps a working automated external defibrillator (AED) on the premises (s. 429.255(3)(a), F.S.). Fire drills are held at the frequency and in the manner required by chapter 69A-40 and the local fire authority, which the Administrator confirms with the fire authority at least annually and records in the Fire Drill Schedule.

definitions.definition: The fire safety requirements in chapter 69A-40, F.A.C., that apply to assisted living facilities and are enforced by the local fire authority or State Fire Marshal.
The city or county fire marshal or fire department that inspects the facility, or the State Fire Marshal where no local authority has jurisdiction.
A practice of the facility's fire alarm and evacuation procedures, including staff roles, conducted as required by the fire authority.
A key kept by the facility that opens all resident bedroom doors.
Automated external defibrillator, a portable device that checks heart rhythm and delivers a shock if needed.

procedures: Before licensure and before opening, the Administrator obtains the fire inspection and documentation from the local fire authority or State Fire Marshal and keeps it in the facility file. No resident is admitted to space that has not been inspected.

The Administrator schedules the annual fire safety inspection with the local fire authority or State Fire Marshal and the annual sanitation inspection with the county health department, and records dates in the regulatory calendar (GOV-02).

Within 30 calendar days of receiving each annual fire and sanitation inspection report, the Administrator sends copies to the AHCA Central Office and records the date and method sent. Deficiencies are corrected by the dates the inspector sets, and corrections are documented.

The Administrator obtains prior approval from AHCA's Field Office before converting any uninspected space to resident use, and prior approval from AHCA's Central Office before changing licensed capacity. No change is made until the approval is in writing.

The Administrator asks the local fire authority in writing for the drill frequency and drill requirements that apply under chapter 69A-40 and records the answer in the Fire Drill Schedule. The Administrator re-confirms this at each annual inspection.

The maintenance director holds fire drills as scheduled, covering all shifts, including the overnight shift, with staff and residents participating as the fire authority requires. Each drill is logged with date, time, shift, evacuation time, staff roles, residents' response, problems noted and corrective actions.

Maintenance staff inspect and test fire alarm devices, smoke detectors, sprinkler systems, fire extinguishers, emergency lighting and exit signs on the schedule that chapter 69A-40 and the manufacturer require, using licensed contractors where required. They keep inspection tags current and record results in the Fire Safety Log.
Maintenance staff check daily that exits, corridors and stairways are clear and unlocked from the inside and that fire doors are not propped open. Any hazard is corrected immediately and recorded.

The facility keeps master keys to all resident bedrooms in a secure but immediately accessible location known to all supervisors. Residents may lock their rooms only if a master key is available. The shift supervisor checks the keys at the start of each shift.

Evacuation floor plans showing exits, routes, extinguisher locations and assembly points are posted on each hall and unit and kept in the emergency binder. The Administrator updates them after any change to the building.

All new employees are trained on the fire plan, the location of alarms, extinguishers and exits, and their role, during preservice orientation and before working alone (STF-03). All staff repeat the training annually.

When the alarm sounds or a fire is discovered, staff follow the posted sequence: rescue residents in immediate danger, sound the alarm and call 911, confine the fire by closing doors, extinguish only if small and safe, and evacuate according to the plan, starting with those closest to danger and those needing help (SAF-09). Staff do a head count at the assembly point against the current census.

After a fire event, alarm activation or drill failure, the Administrator notifies the fire authority as required, files any required report to AHCA (REC-02, SAF-02), and reviews the response with staff within 7 days.

If licensed for 17 or more beds, maintenance staff check the AED monthly for readiness (indicator light, pads and battery dates). The Administrator makes sure staff on every shift know where it is. Staff are trained in First Aid/CPR as required under Rule 59A-36.011 (STF-03).
Smoking, open flame, oxygen use and cooking hazards are controlled under SAF-14 and DL-01, and the facility's smoking rules are posted.
The Administrator reviews fire logs, drill results and inspection findings at least quarterly in the quality assurance meeting (GOV-03).

responsibilities.duty: Obtains inspections, sends reports to AHCA within 30 days, obtains approvals for space or capacity changes, confirms drill frequency with the fire authority, and ensures corrections.
Tests and maintains fire equipment, schedules and leads drills, keeps logs, and checks exits, keys and AED.
Directs staff in a fire or drill, checks master keys at shift start, and accounts for residents.
Know their fire roles, report hazards, take part in drills and follow evacuation procedures.

responsibilities.role: Local fire authority / State Fire Marshal
responsibilities.duty: Inspect for fire safety under chapter 69A-40.

documentation: Fire inspection reports and corrections
Sanitation inspection reports
Proof of sending annual fire and sanitation reports to AHCA Central Office within 30 days
AHCA approvals for capacity change or converted space
Fire Drill Schedule and Fire Drill Log
Fire Safety Log (alarm, sprinkler, extinguisher, emergency lighting tests)
Master key checks
AED check log (17+ beds)
Staff fire and emergency training records
Posted evacuation plans

policies.title: Infection Prevention and Control
policies.applies_to: All staff, volunteers, contractors, and visitors where applicable; Administrator; nursing and housekeeping staff
policies.purpose: To prevent the spread of infection among residents, staff and visitors by following hand hygiene, standard precautions, equipment disinfection, bloodborne pathogen protections and staff training.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] maintains an infection prevention and control program that meets Rule 59A-36.007(10), F.A.C., which requires hand hygiene, standard precautions and disinfection of equipment. Staff follow standard precautions with every resident at all times. All employees receive 1 hour of infection control training before providing personal care, and infection control is part of annual in-service training under Rule 59A-36.011, F.A.C. Staff also complete HIV/AIDS training within 30 days of hire as required by Rule 59A-36.011. The facility follows the OSHA Bloodborne Pathogens Standard, 29 CFR 1910.1030, for staff who may be exposed to blood or other potentially infectious materials. The county health department inspects the facility's sanitation and biomedical waste handling, and the facility cooperates with the inspections and with any health department direction during an outbreak.

definitions.definition: Basic infection-prevention practices used with all residents regardless of diagnosis: hand hygiene, gloves, gown, mask or eye protection when needed, safe injection and sharps practice, safe handling of linen and waste, and cleaning of equipment.
Washing hands with soap and water or using alcohol-based hand rub as appropriate.
Microorganisms in human blood or body fluids that can cause disease, such as hepatitis B, hepatitis C and HIV.
Waste such as sharps and items saturated with blood or body fluids that must be handled and disposed of according to Florida law and county health department requirements.
Two or more related cases of illness among residents or staff, or any number the county health department tells the facility to treat as an outbreak.

procedures: Before an employee gives any personal care, the employee completes 1 hour of infection control training covering standard precautions, hand hygiene, glove use, equipment cleaning, bloodborne pathogens and outbreak reporting. The Administrator records the date in the personnel file (STF-03, STF-05).

Every employee receives HIV/AIDS training within 30 days of hire and completes infection control in-service training each year as required under Rule 59A-36.011. Training dates and content are recorded.

Hand hygiene: staff wash hands with soap and water or use alcohol-based hand rub before and after resident contact, before handling food or medication, after toileting or personal care, after removing gloves, and whenever hands are soiled. Hand sinks and hand rub are kept stocked, and the maintenance director checks them weekly.

Standard precautions: staff treat all blood and body fluids as potentially infectious. They wear gloves for contact with body fluids, broken skin or soiled items; gown and eye protection when splashing is possible; and change gloves between residents and tasks.

Equipment disinfection: shared equipment (thermometers, blood pressure cuffs, glucometers, wheelchairs, shower chairs, lifts) is cleaned and disinfected between residents with an EPA-registered disinfectant, used according to label contact time. Glucometers and any lancing devices are used according to the manufacturer's instructions and never shared without disinfection.

Sharps and waste: used sharps go immediately into puncture-resistant containers that are kept at the point of use. Containers and biomedical waste are removed by a licensed biomedical waste hauler according to county health department and state requirements, and manifests are kept. Regular trash and soiled linen are bagged and handled as the housekeeping plan requires (DL-03).

Exposure control (29 CFR 1910.1030): the Administrator keeps a written exposure control plan listing job duties with possible exposure, personal protective equipment, hepatitis B vaccination offered at no cost to exposed employees within the time OSHA requires, and post-exposure evaluation and follow-up. The plan is reviewed annually.

Exposure incident: an employee who is stuck by a needle or exposed to blood or body fluids washes the area at once, reports to the supervisor, and is referred for medical evaluation. The Administrator records the incident and follow-up and keeps records confidentially (STF-04).

Staff do not work while they have symptoms of a contagious illness (for example fever, vomiting, diarrhea, or an infectious rash) until cleared under the facility's staff illness guidance and employee health policy (STF-04). Employee TB screening follows STF-04.

Residents with signs of infection are reported to the nurse or supervisor, who notifies the physician and the representative (HS-04) and applies any needed extra precautions such as isolating the resident to the room, additional PPE, dedicated equipment, and meals in the room. Precautions are recorded in the resident's record.
At admission and as part of assessment, the nurse records the resident's immunization status and offers or arranges immunizations as ordered or recommended, subject to the resident's choice.
Food safety: staff who handle food follow DL-01 and complete food handler training. Staff with diarrhea or vomiting do not handle food.

Housekeeping: environmental surfaces, bathrooms and high-touch areas are cleaned and disinfected on the housekeeping schedule, and immediately after contamination. Laundry is handled as DL-03 describes, with soiled items handled using gloves and not shaken.

Outbreak response: if the nurse or supervisor suspects an outbreak, they tell the Administrator at once. The Administrator notifies the county health department and follows its direction, notifies physicians, residents and representatives, limits visitation or group activities as directed, and reports to AHCA where reporting is required (REC-02).

The Administrator reviews infection trends, exposures, outbreaks and staff compliance at least quarterly in the QA process and updates procedures as needed (GOV-03). Records of inspections by the county health department are kept in the facility file.

responsibilities.duty: Ensures the program, training, supplies and exposure control plan are in place, coordinates with the county health department, and reports outbreaks.
Reviews infection signs, oversees precautions, trains staff, and records infection and immunization data.
Follow standard precautions, perform hand hygiene, disinfect equipment, and report symptoms and exposures.
Clean and disinfect the environment and handle linen and waste safely.
Keeps sinks, hand rub dispensers, sharps containers and waste contracts working and supplied.

documentation: Infection control training records (1 hour before personal care; annual in-service)
HIV/AIDS training records (within 30 days of hire)
Written exposure control plan and hepatitis B vaccination or declination records
Exposure incident reports and follow-up
Biomedical waste hauler contract and manifests
Equipment cleaning logs and housekeeping schedules
Infection and outbreak logs and health department correspondence
County health department inspection reports

policies.title: Smoking, Visitation and Pets
policies.applies_to: All residents, visitors, volunteers, contracted providers and staff at [AGENCY NAME] at [ADDRESS]
policies.purpose: To set clear, written rules for smoking, visitation and animals that protect resident safety and respect resident rights, and to meet the requirement for a written visitation policy and published house rules.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] maintains a written visitation policy as required for the licensure application and by Rule 59A-36.015(1)(v), F.A.C. (s. 408.823, F.S.). The facility also keeps written house rules under Rule 59A-36.007, F.A.C. Visiting hours are posted in the house rules, and the house rules are given to each resident at admission. Residents may receive visitors and may use the telephone privately. A resident's visitors may be limited only at the resident's own request, for a documented safety or infection-control reason, or by a court order. Smoking is allowed only in the designated area(s) approved under the fire safety requirements that apply to the building, and never where oxygen is stored or in use. Resident-owned pets and facility animals are governed by the house rules. Service animals are accommodated as required by state and federal disability law. The house rules do not conflict with the Resident Bill of Rights, which is posted in the facility.

definitions.definition: Any person who enters the facility to see a resident, including family, friends, clergy, legal counsel, the long-term care ombudsman and an essential caregiver chosen by the resident.

An outdoor location identified by the Administrator, with approved ash receptacles and signage, that meets applicable fire safety requirements and is away from entrances, oxygen storage and combustible materials.
An animal individually trained to do work or perform tasks for a person with a disability. It is not treated as a pet under the house rules.
The written rules of the facility on matters such as visiting hours, smoking and pets, which are given to residents and do not take away any resident right.

procedures: The Administrator writes and approves the visitation policy and the smoking and pet sections of the house rules before licensure. The Administrator reviews them at least annually and whenever a law, rule or AHCA directive changes.

The house rules state the visiting hours, which are open to residents' preferences, how visitors sign in, and how a resident may request a visit outside those hours. The Administrator posts the visiting hours in a common area and includes them in the admission package (ADM-02).

At admission the Admissions Coordinator reviews the visitation, smoking and pet rules with the resident and representative. The resident or representative signs an acknowledgment, which is filed in the resident record.

Staff greet visitors, ask them to sign the visitor log, and direct them to the resident. Visits take place in the resident's room, common areas or outdoors, whichever the resident prefers. Staff ensure privacy on request.

Staff never refuse a visit because of the visitor's identity or the resident's payment source. A visit may be limited only on the resident's request, for a documented safety or infection-control reason, or by court order. The Administrator or designee approves and documents any limit, including the reason and the date, and tells the resident and representative.

Staff allow the long-term care ombudsman, AHCA surveyors, the resident's physician and hospice, and legal counsel access to the resident in line with RR-02. The Administrator follows s. 408.823, F.S. and AHCA direction on essential caregiver visitation, including during an infection outbreak (SAF-13) or emergency.
Staff do not allow visitors who are impaired, abusive or disruptive to remain. The shift supervisor documents the event and notifies the Administrator the same day.

The Administrator designates smoking areas in writing, consistent with the fire safety requirements that apply to the building. Signs prohibit smoking indoors and anywhere oxygen is in use or stored. 'No Smoking – Oxygen in Use' signs are posted where oxygen is present.

During assessment (ADM-03) the nurse or Administrator identifies residents who smoke. Residents who cannot smoke safely get a service plan entry (ADM-04), such as supervision, a smoking apron or staff-held lighters. Staff do not give residents tobacco or lighters in violation of the plan.
Staff check smoking areas each shift for hazards and empty ash receptacles into metal containers with lids. Maintenance (DL-03) inspects the receptacles weekly.

Resident-owned pets are allowed only as the house rules permit. Before a pet moves in, the Administrator confirms a current rabies and other vaccination record, that the resident or representative will feed and clean up after it, and that other residents are not adversely affected. A pet agreement is signed and filed.

Pets stay out of food preparation areas. They are kept leashed or contained in common areas. If a pet endangers anyone, the Administrator may require its removal after notifying the resident or representative in writing.
Staff admit service animals without a pet agreement, as state and federal disability law require. Staff may ask only whether the animal is required because of a disability and what task it performs.

The Administrator logs visitation, smoking and pet complaints and reviews them quarterly in the QA process (GOV-03). Residents may use the grievance process in RR-02 for any complaint about these rules.
Staff receive training on this policy at orientation (STF-03). Retraining follows any substantiated violation.

responsibilities.duty: Writes, posts and reviews the visitation policy and house rules, approves any visitor limits and pet agreements, designates smoking areas, and makes sure the rules are consistent with the Resident Bill of Rights.
Reviews the rules with each resident at admission and files the signed acknowledgment.
Enforces the rules on shift, documents any visitor issue or smoking violation, and reports to the Administrator.
Inspects smoking areas and ash receptacles and keeps required signage in place.
Welcome visitors, protect resident privacy, follow smoking service plans and report hazards.

documentation: Written visitation policy and house rules with revision dates
Signed resident acknowledgment of house rules
Visitor log
Documentation of any visitation limit, with the reason and notice to the resident
Smoking service plan entries
Pet agreements and vaccination records
Smoking area inspection log
Quarterly QA review minutes

policies.title: Food Service and Therapeutic Diets
policies.applies_to: All residents, dietary staff, contracted food service vendors, and staff who serve or assist with meals at [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To make sure residents receive safe, nutritionally adequate meals and snacks, that special and therapeutic diets are provided as ordered, and that the facility tells prospective residents what food service and diets it can accommodate.
policies.policy: This policy meets Rule 59A-36.006(3)(a)5., F.A.C. — food service and the ability of the facility to accommodate special diets. The facility's food service and its ability to accommodate special diets are described in the admission package, and each prospective resident is told which diets the facility can and cannot provide. Under Rule 59A-36.012, F.A.C., the Administrator designates in writing a person responsible for food service. Menus are based on the USDA Dietary Guidelines and are reviewed at least annually by a dietitian or nutritionist. Menus are planned at least one week ahead, and menus as served are kept for six months. Therapeutic diets are provided as ordered by a licensed practitioner. Meals and snacks are served within the meal-interval limits in the rule. The facility keeps a three-day supply of nonperishable food. County health department inspection reports are kept for two years. Staff who handle food are trained under Rule 59A-36.011, F.A.C.

definitions.definition: The person named in writing by the Administrator as responsible for menus, food safety, diets and the food supply.
A diet ordered by a licensed practitioner for a medical condition, such as diabetic, low-sodium, renal, pureed or mechanically altered.
The record of what was actually served at each meal and snack, including substitutions.
At least a three-day supply of shelf-stable food and water kept on hand for emergencies (see SAF-05 and SAF-06).

procedures: The Administrator names a food service designee in writing before opening and whenever the designee changes. The appointment letter is kept in the administrative file.
The food service designee develops menus based on the USDA Dietary Guidelines. A dietitian or nutritionist reviews and signs the menus at least annually, and the signed review is kept on file.
The designee plans menus at least one week ahead and dates them. The current week's menu is posted where residents can see it or is given to residents on request.
Dietary staff record each meal as actually served, including any substitution, on the menu-as-served record. Records are kept at least six months.
Meals and snacks are offered within the meal-interval limits in Rule 59A-36.012, F.A.C. Staff plan the day's schedule and snacks so that no resident goes beyond the allowed interval.

During pre-admission screening (ADM-01) the Administrator or designee asks about the prospective resident's diet needs. The facility accepts only residents whose diet orders it can accommodate and documents the decision.
The admission package (ADM-02) describes meal times, snacks, choices, guest meals and the diets the facility can and cannot accommodate. The Admissions Coordinator reviews this with the resident.

When a practitioner orders a therapeutic diet, staff obtain the written order (or the diet is shown on the health assessment), record it in the resident's service plan (ADM-04) and give the order to the kitchen the same day. The kitchen posts diet lists in a place not visible to the public.

Staff serve therapeutic diets exactly as ordered and observe how each resident eats. They report refusals, weight change, choking, or difficulty swallowing to the nurse or Administrator, who notifies the practitioner under HS-04.
Residents may choose among menu items and may decline food. Staff offer alternatives and document repeated refusals.

Food is purchased from approved sources, stored at safe temperatures, labeled and dated. Food contact surfaces and equipment are cleaned and sanitized. Staff are trained in safe food handling and food service continuing education under Rule 59A-36.011, F.A.C.

If a contractor provides food service, the Administrator keeps the written contract and documentation that the contractor meets this policy and county health department requirements. The designee still monitors menus, diets and food safety.

The designee keeps a three-day supply of nonperishable food and water, rotates it and checks it quarterly. The supply is part of the emergency plan (SAF-05) and is checked again at the start of hurricane season.
The Administrator keeps county health department inspection reports for two years and makes them available to AHCA. Any citation is corrected promptly and reviewed in QA (GOV-03).
The designee reviews resident satisfaction with meals at each resident council or quarterly meeting. Staff document the comments and any changes made.

responsibilities.duty: Appoints the food service designee, oversees contracts, and makes sure the facility accepts only residents whose diets it can accommodate.
Plans menus, arranges the annual dietitian review, oversees storage and sanitation, maintains the emergency food supply and keeps the required records.
Reviews menus at least annually for nutritional adequacy and consistency with the USDA Dietary Guidelines.
Verify diet orders, update the service plan, and monitor residents on therapeutic diets.
Serve meals as planned and ordered, observe intake, and report concerns.

documentation: Written appointment of food service designee
Menus (planned) and annual dietitian or nutritionist review
Menus as served (kept 6 months)
Diet orders and diet list
Admission package statement of food service and special-diet capability
Emergency food supply inventory
County health department inspection reports (kept 2 years)
Food service contract, if any
Staff training records

policies.title: Activities and Social Programming
policies.applies_to: All residents and activity, direct care and administrative staff at [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To provide a regular, resident-centered program of social, recreational and other activities that meets the state's minimum schedule, honors each resident's choices, and is clearly described to prospective residents.
policies.policy: This policy meets Rule 59A-36.006(3)(a)8., F.A.C. — social and leisure activities generally offered by the facility. In accordance with Rule 59A-36.007(2), F.A.C., [AGENCY NAME] provides an activities program of at least 12 hours per week, offered across at least 6 days per week. Residents choose whether and how to take part. Activities are matched to residents' interests and abilities, and a description of the activities generally offered is included in the admission package. Residents are never required to work or perform services for the facility without compensation, and participation in any activity is voluntary.

definitions.definition: Planned social, recreational, physical, creative, cognitive, spiritual and community activities offered to residents.
The staff member designated by the Administrator to plan, schedule and document activities.
The resident's right to take part in, decline or suggest activities without penalty.

procedures: The Administrator designates an activities coordinator in writing. The coordinator is trained in resident rights and in working with residents who have cognitive or mobility limitations (STF-03).

At admission and at each reassessment, the coordinator or nurse completes an interest profile covering the resident's hobbies, faith, routines, language, abilities and preferences. It is filed in the resident record.
The coordinator builds a monthly calendar with at least 12 hours of planned activity a week, spread over at least 6 days. The Administrator reviews and approves the calendar before the month begins.

The calendar includes a range of activity types: social, physical, creative, cognitive, spiritual and community. It includes options for residents who stay in their rooms and for residents with dementia (HS-05).
The calendar is posted in a common area and given to residents and representatives on request. Large print and translated copies are available (RR-07).
The activity schedule and a description of the activities generally offered are included in the admission package (ADM-02). The Admissions Coordinator reviews them with each prospective resident.

Staff invite residents to take part, but may not require or penalize anyone for declining. Residents may suggest activities, outings or speakers. The coordinator documents requests and responds within a reasonable time.
Activities are held in accessible spaces, with assistive devices and staff assistance as needed. Staff provide one-to-one visits for residents who cannot attend group events.
The coordinator records each activity held (date, time, length, staff) and who took part on an attendance log. Declined invitations are noted.
The coordinator reviews attendance monthly. Residents with little or no participation are referred to the nurse or Administrator to find barriers and update the service plan (ADM-04).

Residents are never asked to do work for the facility. A resident may, voluntarily, do personal chores and be paid fairly under a written agreement signed by the resident, consistent with RR-01. No resident is penalized for refusing.
Outings and events off-site follow transportation procedures (DL-04), with consents and staffing in place.
Supplies and equipment are bought within the approved budget. The coordinator checks safety, such as craft materials and exercise equipment, before each use.
The Administrator reviews the program quarterly with resident input (resident council or survey) and reports the findings in QA (GOV-03).

responsibilities.duty: Approves the monthly calendar, ensures the 12-hour / 6-day minimum is met, and funds supplies and staffing.
Completes interest profiles, plans and documents activities, and monitors participation.
Help residents to and from activities and support residents who prefer in-room activity.
Provides the activities description in the admission package.

documentation: Monthly activity calendars
Resident interest profiles
Activity attendance logs
Resident requests and responses
Admission package activities description
Quarterly program review notes

policies.title: Housekeeping, Laundry and Maintenance
policies.applies_to: All housekeeping, laundry, maintenance and direct care staff, and all resident rooms and common areas at [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To keep the building clean, safe, sanitary and in good repair, to furnish each resident's room and provide linens and laundry service, and to prepare the facility for county health, fire and AHCA inspections.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] maintains the premises, equipment and grounds in good repair and in a clean, sanitary condition. The building meets the Florida Building Code and the fire standards of chapter 69A-40, F.A.C., as required by Rule 59A-36.014, F.A.C. The facility furnishes each resident room with at least a bed with a mattress of at least 36 x 72 inches, a closet or wardrobe, a dresser, a nightstand or table, a lamp and a wastebasket. Residents may bring their own furniture if it is safe and fits. The facility provides clean linens and laundry service. The facility keeps master keys to resident rooms and secures them. Under Rule 59A-36.005, F.A.C., the county health department inspects sanitation, food hygiene and biomedical waste, the local fire authority or State Fire Marshal inspects fire safety, and AHCA inspects all other areas. The facility corrects all deficiencies promptly.

definitions.definition: A key or access device that opens every resident room, kept by the facility for emergency and safety access.
Scheduled inspection and servicing of building systems and equipment to prevent failures.
Waste such as sharps and items contaminated with blood or body fluids, handled under the rules enforced by the county health department.

procedures: The Administrator designates a Maintenance Director and a Housekeeping Lead in writing. The Maintenance Director keeps a written preventive maintenance schedule for HVAC, plumbing, electrical, generator, fire systems, elevators, and resident-room equipment.

Before each admission, housekeeping and maintenance inspect the room. The room must contain a bed with a 36 x 72 inch or larger mattress, closet or wardrobe, dresser, nightstand or table, lamp and wastebasket, all clean and in good repair. The Housekeeping Lead signs a room-readiness checklist.

Residents may bring furniture and belongings. The Administrator or designee checks that items are safe, do not block exits or walkways, and meet fire safety requirements. The resident's personal items are listed in the inventory under RR-04.
Housekeeping cleans resident rooms, bathrooms and common areas on a written schedule, and more often when soiled. Staff use approved disinfectants as labeled and follow standard precautions (SAF-13).

The facility supplies clean bed linens and towels and changes them at least weekly and whenever soiled. Staff handle soiled laundry with gloves, bag it at the point of use, and keep it separate from clean linen and from food areas.

The facility provides laundry service for personal clothing. Staff label items, return laundry promptly and report lost items under RR-04. Residents who prefer to do their own laundry are assisted as the service plan states.

Maintenance staff log all repair requests, with dates, in a work-order log. Staff may report problems verbally or in writing. Urgent hazards (no water, no power, broken locks, fire system trouble) are fixed or made safe immediately and reported to the Administrator at once.

Maintenance checks monthly that fire extinguishers, smoke detectors, alarms, emergency lighting, exit signs and generators are working, and keeps results in the safety log (SAF-12, SAF-10). Damaged items are repaired or replaced at once.
The Administrator keeps master keys in a secure, controlled location and logs who has access. Staff knock and ask permission before entering a resident room, except in an emergency.

The Administrator contracts for pest control and for biomedical waste disposal with licensed vendors. Sharps and contaminated waste are placed in proper containers and removed as required. Vendor service reports are filed.
Hazardous chemicals are labeled, stored in locked areas away from food and medication, and Safety Data Sheets are kept on site. Staff are trained to handle them at orientation (STF-03).

The Administrator keeps the Florida Building Code and chapter 69A-40 fire inspection reports, county health department reports and AHCA survey reports on file. Any cited deficiency is corrected on schedule and the correction is documented.

Before any renovation or repair that could affect safety or resident care, the Administrator confirms that required permits and plan approvals are in place and that residents are protected from dust, noise and unsafe areas.
The Administrator reviews work orders, inspection findings and cleanliness audits quarterly in QA (GOV-03).

responsibilities.duty: Ensures the building and furnishings meet standards, controls master keys, and corrects inspection findings.
Runs preventive maintenance, work orders, safety system checks and vendor contracts.
Supervises cleaning, linen and laundry service, and room readiness.
Report repair needs and unsafe conditions, and assist residents with their rooms and personal laundry.

documentation: Preventive maintenance schedule and completed logs
Work-order log
Room-readiness checklists
Cleaning schedules and audits
Safety system check logs
Master key access log
Pest control and biomedical waste vendor reports
County health department, fire authority and AHCA inspection reports and corrective actions

policies.title: Transportation
policies.applies_to: All residents, drivers, direct care staff and the Administrator at [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To make sure residents have access to transportation for health care and community activities, that availability and any additional cost are disclosed in writing before admission, and that transport is safe and accessible.
policies.policy: This policy meets Rule 59A-36.006(3)(a)6., F.A.C. — the availability of transportation and additional costs to the resident, if any. [AGENCY NAME] arranges transportation for residents to health care appointments as Rule 59A-36.007(3), F.A.C. requires. The admission package and the resident contract state whether the facility provides transportation, what is provided and any additional charge. Under Rule 59A-36.018, F.A.C., additional charges need an itemized statement and a signed, dated addendum. If the facility holds an Extended Congregate Care license, it also arranges transportation to community activities on a resident's request. Transportation is provided without discrimination and with reasonable accommodation for residents with disabilities, consistent with the Americans with Disabilities Act (42 USC 12101). Emergency transport is by calling 911.

definitions.definition: Scheduling, providing or helping the resident obtain a ride, either with a facility vehicle, a contracted or Medicaid-covered provider, or a family member.
A fee for transportation that is not included in the base rate and is set out in the contract or an addendum.
A vehicle equipped to safely carry residents who use wheelchairs or other mobility devices.

procedures: The Administrator decides which transportation the facility will provide directly, which it will arrange through other providers, and what, if anything, it charges. The decision is written down before the first admission.

The Admissions Coordinator states in the admission package and in the resident contract whether transportation is available, the types of trips covered, any limits (such as distance or hours), and any additional cost. Any extra charge is set out in an itemized statement and a signed, dated addendum.

The nurse or designee asks every resident at admission and at each reassessment about transportation needs for medical visits, dialysis, therapy, community, and faith activities, and records them in the service plan (ADM-04).
Appointments are put on the appointment calendar. The designated staff member schedules transportation at least [NUMBER] business days ahead, or as soon as the appointment is made.
For residents with Medicaid managed care, staff help the resident or representative to use the transportation benefit of the resident's plan or other covered resources when available.

Residents who need an escort are accompanied by staff, a family member or another person named in the service plan. The escort carries the face sheet, medication list, advance directive or DNRO (RR-05) and the emergency contacts.

Staff tell the resident's practitioner of any special needs before the visit. After the visit, staff obtain visit notes and orders, and the nurse or designee updates the resident record and service plan.
If the facility has an ECC license, staff arrange transportation to community activities on a resident's request. Staff document the request, the arrangement made and any cost.
Drivers of facility vehicles hold a valid Florida driver license and have passed the required background screening (STF-02). The Administrator checks driving records at hire and annually.
Facility vehicles are insured (GOV-05), maintained and inspected on a set schedule. Maintenance logs are kept. A vehicle that fails an inspection is taken out of service.
Staff secure wheelchairs and other mobility devices and use seat belts for all riders. Residents are assisted in and out and are never left unattended in a vehicle.

The facility makes reasonable accommodations for residents with disabilities, including ramp- or lift-equipped transport, extra assistance and extra time. If the facility cannot provide an accessible vehicle, staff help arrange an accessible alternative and do not deny the service because of disability.

In an emergency or if a resident's condition changes during a trip, staff call 911 and notify the Administrator, the resident's representative and the practitioner under HS-04. The event is documented under SAF-02.
The Administrator reviews missed appointments, transport complaints and incidents quarterly in QA (GOV-03).

responsibilities.duty: Sets transportation availability and charges, ensures contract disclosures, and oversees vehicles, drivers and insurance.
Discloses transportation availability and any extra cost in the package and contract, and obtains the signed addendum if charges apply.
Identifies transport needs, schedules rides and escorts, and updates the record after appointments.
Transport residents safely, follow securement procedures and report incidents.

documentation: Admission package and resident contract transportation disclosure
Itemized statement and signed, dated addendum for extra charges
Appointment calendar and transport schedule
Service plan entries for transportation needs
Driver license and screening records
Vehicle maintenance and insurance records
Incident reports for transport events

policies.title: Staffing Levels and Supervision
policies.applies_to: Administrator, managers, all direct care, supervisory, nursing and contracted staff, and staffing agencies at [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] always has enough qualified staff on duty to meet residents' needs, meets or exceeds the state minimum weekly staff hours, and keeps awake overnight staff, trained staff and clear supervision at all times.
